utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning everybody. Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here. From amongst the Defence teams I only notice the absence of Mr. Haynes. Prosecution, it's Mr. Vanderpuye and Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I would like to introduce a new legal assistant who will be working with our team, Ms. Marie-Claude Fournier from Montreal. She'd be doing articles with our legal team. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, you seem to be breeding legal assistants. Good morning to you, madam. You come from a beautiful city which I love. Welcome, you're most welcome to the team and to the trial. Thank you. So shall we start with the new witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel, everybody. Your Honour, we're prepared to proceed with the new witness. There is an outstanding 65 ter motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You are right. There is an outstanding motion. What's the position of the Defence teams on that? Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We object. We object on the grounds that we have objected on throughout this proceeding for a year and a half and we've not been successful but we still object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hope springs eternal. Any other remarks? Okay. Yes. No, no, no. I just want the details of the motion, that's all. So we're dealing with the Prosecution notice of disclosure pursuant to Rule 94 bis, a motion for leave to amend the 65 ter exhibit list, which was filed on Friday, 25th of January of this year. We've heard the objection in general terms raised by Mr. Meek for the Beara Defence team. I take it it's only for the Beara Defence team, Mr. Meek, is it? Isn't it? You're not -- are you speaking for everyone or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm speaking for Beara Defence team and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So the Trial Chamber, having confirmed comes to the conclusion to grant the motion to add to the 65 ter list the -- the documents mentioned in the same motion. So we can proceed now. Any -- there are no protective measures or any other --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, there are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- preliminary matter you wish to discuss in relation to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, except that given the time constraint that we have with presenting his testimony, I would ask to lead him on at least some preliminary issues so that we can expedite the presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you have been made aware that there is a time limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you stick to that? Not a minute more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, Mr. Parsons, and welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're about to start your testimony here. You need to be sworn in before that. Madam Usher is going to hand you a text of our solemn declaration. Please read it aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Vanderpuye will ask you a few questions and then there will be cross-examinations after that. Mr. Vanderpuye, your half an hour starts from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you would please just state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Thomas John Parsons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You prior to today had submitted or provided copy of your curriculum vitae; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, that is 65 ter 3172. Now, with respect to your educational background, it is correct that you earned your BS in -- BS degree in physics from the University of Chicago in 1982?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it is correct that you earned your Ph.D. from the University of Washington department of biochemistry in 1989; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you hear that? Both of you please comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Since then is it correct that you've been engaged professionally from 1989 as a post doctoral fellow at the laboratory of molecular systematics at the Smithsonian institution in 1989 through 1992, right up through the position of chief scientist for the United States armed forces DNA identification laboratory from 2000 to 2006; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you're currently employed by the ICMP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And your position there is the director of forensic sciences?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you been there since about March of 2006?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to your position at the ICMP, I want to ask you two questions. First is, if you could briefly describe what the mission of the ICMP is; and secondly, if you could describe briefly what your duties and responsibilities are as the director of forensic sciences.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The ICMP's principal mission is to assist governments with the issue of missing persons, and this is accomplished in a number of means. One is through governmental relations that works with governments to establish laws and policies and hold them to account for the problem of the missing. Another is a civil society initiative which is to mobilise family groups and provide them with the ability to -- to meet and with funding so that they can have a voice in the government. And then the third pillar is assistance with forensic sciences in terms of actually providing identifications and we have a very strong integrated programme of forensic sciences involving both DNA and traditional methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in terms of your responsibilities and duties as director of forensic sciences could you briefly outline to the Court what those are?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please make pauses between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I supervise three main forensic science divisions one is called examinations and excavations and that relates anthropology and archaeology for assistance with recovery of bodies from mass graves and other areas. Anthropological analysis to term things like age, sex, and stature of the victims. Pathological analysis to determine cause of death. This type of thing. A second area is the DNA laboratory system where we perform DNA typing and that principally is to match DNA profiles from the skeletal remains that are recovered to blood reference samples of the family of the missing and make matches in that manner. The third organisational division that I oversee is called the identification coordination division and that is a link between the samples and the genetic data. So all samples go through the identification coordination division. They enter a very homogeneous process. The samples are distributed to the DNA laboratory. The DNA typing results go back to the identification coordination division and matches are made and that's how we perform the DNA identification process.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in terms of your supervision of the laboratory, DNA laboratories, can you tell us what type of testing or what typing is done in those laboratories?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, we use a very standard type of DNA fingerprinting type profiling which is the amplification of autosomal nuclear short tandem repeat loci. This is quite widely used globally for the -- for the application of human identification and is the type of thing that's the basis of criminal or offender databases, for example, in the United States and the UK.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, is that manner of testing consistent with the industry standards presently?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is the -- the way that testing is carried out detailed in your report, that is the report methodology report from 2001 to 2008?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes. That contains a relevant SOP, standard operating procedures in the DNA laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And for the record that is 65 ter 3174. Now is the testing that's conducted by the -- by the laboratories, is that conducted in accordance with certain pre-existing standard operating procedures?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are those procedures referred to in your report?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how do those procedures relate to the use and operation of the equipment used to conduct these tests?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: They -- they define the -- the actions and procedures that the analysts perform in order to achieve the DNA testing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do they also relate to issues outside of the use of the equipment such as the handling of samples, the making of matches, the calculation of statistical data and probabilities and things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: They do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what if you -- if you could tell us, what is the relationship of the standard operating procedures to the reliability of the results achieved in the testing that is done at the lab?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, the standard operating procedures merely -- or -- or define what it is that we do. The -- the -- the reliability of the results is dependent upon the system in place and -- and a wide range of checks and balances that go out throughout the entire process.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us when it is that the ICMP laboratory system became operational?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: DNA laboratories have been active since 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And since 2001 has there been any change in the way that ICMP has carried out this nuclear STR testing, typing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, I have to say in -- in all laboratories where this type of work done there's -- there's constant minor evolution in terms of the exact steps and methodologies, et cetera, but I think probably the best general question -- answer to your question is that in 2002 we -- we shifted instrumentational platforms from what was previously more or less essentially the industry standard to -- to a new instrument platform and -- and we also changed the extraction methodology that was used. The extraction is where you take the bone sample and perform chemical manipulations to retrieve relatively pure DNA. And when the ICMP got started they were using what was -- what was widely used in the world and then performed additional experimentation and devised a new more efficient method has really since 2002 has been the basis of our very high success rate with this type of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you refer to a success rate with respect to this material, are you referring to the ability to extract DNA?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The ability to successfully extract DNA and then perform a polymerase chain reaction amplification of the DNA to result in the DNA profiles that we use for genetic comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And that would be commonly known as, well, PCR testing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yeah, PCR testing of STR loci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in the simplest terms, what is the effect of these changes on the reliability of the testing process and the results that are obtained?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- in general I don't think that the minor procedural changes affect the fundamental reliability. As I said, in -- in transferring the primary instrumentation platform - and these are commercially available high-tech laser-driven instruments - the sensitivity of the newer model that we switched over to in 2002 is higher and that gives rise to an increased success rate. And as I mentioned also the more highly optimised DNA extraction methodology that we employed in 2002 has given us a higher success rate on the bone samples. Sometimes the DNA is simply too degraded to obtain material, but in the vast majority of cases we are able to get a robust DNA and make the comparisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Kwon and I were engaging in telepathy. I am very much suspecting that you are having problems catching up with the witness in particular; is that correct, interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you kindly slow down. It's very difficult. The interpreters' job is a very difficult one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us is the ICMP currently an accredited laboratory facility?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes. We have ISO 17025 accreditation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when was this accreditation obtained?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: In October of 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And has there been any material departure from the way testing was carried out before this accreditation and the way it's carried out now?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the procedure you briefly went over that at the very beginning of your testimony, but in terms of identification does ICMP compare the DNA of these -- of bone samples with the DNA of blood donors?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the bone samples that you test, do you receive them from a single source, multiple sources?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: We get them from multiple sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the information that you receive concerning these sources, is that also provided to you by -- by agencies other than -- other than your own?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: In many instances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And what I mean by that is I'm referring to grave sites, locations where the bone samples are recovered.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does the ICMP independently verify the accuracy of this information?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: As a general rule that is not within our responsibility. However, very often our teams are deployed to the site and oversee the technical operations at the site so we're not in many instances wholly dissociated from that process, but that is not our primary purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in your experience in handling this information or dealing with this information, do you have any reason to believe that the information such as the location of the recovery of samples and information of that nature is inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the Srebrenica-related missing particularly, how is the location and place of disappearance denoted in the ICMP database?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, I should mention that -- that for individuals reported missing from anywhere in Bosnia regarding any event, the information that we get comes from the family members of the missing. So to -- to associate it with -- with Srebrenica, that would have been information that the family provided to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now with respect to the information as to where the person was missing or the date that they became missing, is that represented in the database of the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if I could briefly have up in e-court 65 ter 3002A, 3002A. It should not be broadcast. I don't know if we can bring that a little bit into better focus. It's a bit blurry on the screen. Are you able to read that, Dr. Parsons?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Actually, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still, I don't know how much that is helpful. If -- if it's properly focused, yes. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No. It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It was much better before. Yeah. I think it's decent enough now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you would, could you briefly just take us through -- I don't think we have to deal with the names or date of births but perhaps we could start with the column that's indicated "protocol ID" and tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, this is a list that we provided that indicates individuals that we have issued DNA match reports relating to the Srebrenica event. In the protocol ID number is -- is simply an identifier of a particular DNA match report that was issued for that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And next is a case ID.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That number indicates the -- the identifier of the particular bone sample that was submitted to our laboratory for DNA identification. So that is what it was called when we received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If we could move a little bit to the right. The next you see is the ID ICMP.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That simply is a serially increasing number that indicates what number historically of match report this was. So the one at the top was the fourth one that the ICMP ever generated; et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the information concerning the site name, is that information that is provided to you by the provider of the sample?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could go all the way to the right, please. All right. Here we see D of Dis, Date of disappearance; and P of Dis, Place of disappearance. With respect to these entries there is a consistent date of 11/7/1995. Can you tell us why that is.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I mentioned that we get the information on missing persons from families. That's our -- our job is to return their loved ones to them. And we record by our expert interviewer teams who obtain the genetic samples and meet with the families and ascertain who they are and properly record all the information; they ask the date of disappearance and the place of disappearance of the missing persons. In the case of Srebrenica, the decision was made to go with two nominal -- with nominal designations in these areas because the confused nature of the events at that time made it very difficult to obtain an internally consistent date of disappearance or place of disappearance regionally. So someone may have been last seen by one member of the family taking off through the forest to try to reach Tuzla and seen by -- last seen by another member of the family somewhere along at that route or something. And so because we deal with multiple family members, we have ascribed a nominal date and place of disappearance. And the place of disappearance has actually two categories: Either Potocari, indicating that they remained behind and went missing; or forest, indicating that they took the overland escape -- attempted escape route.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that this -- this particular set of data indicates certain matches, DNA matches.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in terms of obtaining a match, can you briefly describe what the process is that's involved for -- for the Court?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Blood samples are taken from family members of the missing. In many instances we get as many as we can usually and on average have three different family members associated with each missing person. Those profiles are typed in an entirely anonymous fashion and the genetic profiles are uploaded to a DNA database. Then as the bone samples are processed again in a -- in a totally anonymised manner, after the profile of the bone sample is obtained it is run via computer against the entire database of family reference profiles and we are able to then identify genetic consistencies that are genetic patterns that are consistent with familial relationship. And once such a match has been made to a given named individual, then we bring all the genetic profiles for that missing person into a single calculation and we perform -- using a computer programme that is one of the industry standards arrive at a final statistical surety that -- of that relationship of the bone profile to that family.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of the statistical relationship, that is the level of surety that is required in order to -- to obtain a match, what does that have to be?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: For samples that proceed in the manner that I just described which is a vast, vast majority of them, we have a minimum statistical surety of 99.95 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that the case even where there is presumptive evidence of identification?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: For a small number of samples regionally we have provision for a pathologist to have a strong presumption of identity prior to submitting for DNA typing. So if a sample is submitted to us with a name associated, we strongly -- in effect saying we strongly believe this sample comes from a particular named individual, then we will do a very directed comparison against that named individual and either issue an exclusion report saying, No, your presumption was wrong or provide a statistic of inclusion. And we will in those instances issue a match report at a 99 per cent certainty, giving weight to the additional presumption that was in place prior to the DNA submission. But those are quite exceptional with relation to this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this list we're talking about, do you recall when that list was provided to the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: It was in October of 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the Srebrenica-related missing, did the ICMP obtain a certain number of unique DNA profiles for which it was able to obtain these matches as you've indicated?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. With regard to the Srebrenica-related missing, did the ICMP obtain a certain number of unique DNA profiles for which it was able to make these matches?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall how many such matches there were?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Sir, I don't right at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 3005 in e-court, please. It also should not be broadcasted as well. Okay. If we could just blow it up a little bit. That's great.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would like to just refer you to the second to last sentence of paragraph 2. It reads: "These profiles represent 5.280 different individuals," and that is out of 8.445 bone samples. And then it says "From these 5.280 individuals ICMP has determined family matches for 5.055." This is a letter that was written by you. Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is it accurate with respect to the number of identifications -- matches, I should say, that were made?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: As of November 30th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you aware of whether there were unique DNA profiles that were obtained for a number of individuals for which the ICMP was unable to make matches?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this is again with reference to the Srebrenica-related missing.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall approximately how many individuals there were?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That number changes all the time. With reference to the document we're looking at, November 30th, we see a difference of -- there are family matches for 5.055 of the 5.280 profiles. So there's some 200 at that time that we did not have matches for.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Are you aware of whether or not the ICMP actually furnished the ICTY with more updated information with respect to the number of profiles for which matches could not be obtained?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I believe that the answer to that would be no. At one point a different list was submitted that -- that had had actually more names on it and I believe that that information was prior to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: And what has happened is we've made more identifications and therefore the number that we have not identified is lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, with respect to the individuals that you were not able to obtain matches for, how is it that you made the determination that they were Srebrenica related?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The principal, most direct answer from our own experience to that is that those bone samples came to us from graves from which many other individuals who were missing from Srebrenica were identified. So these were secondary mass graves for which we've identified many, many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, given your experience and your expertise in the area of DNA testing, can you tell us in your opinion is the DNA identification and matching process that is conducted by the ICMP reliable to a reasonable degree of scientific certainty?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, it is very robust.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I thank you very much, Dr. Parsons. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence agreed that Mr. Meek will go first and then we will be -- Ms. Tapuskovic will follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's not waste time. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Parsons. How are you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: My name is Chris Meek and I'm one the attorneys for Ljubisa Beara and we are under quite some time restraints you understand so, if possible, I would like to get some yes or no answers and move along. First off, in regards to the most recent methodology report, 2001 to 2008, which is 65 ter 3174, on page 1 you state that one of your duties includes the supervision of exhumation and excavation division; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: However, on page 2, point 3 of that report says that the ICMP -- ICMP does not generally conduct excavations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The ICMP is very regularly involved in excavations. I think the word "conduct" is what we may be concerned with here. I'm sorry not to give a yes or no answer, but the actual excavation of the grave sites is under the authority not of the ICMP. We provide technological assistance at sites very routinely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So tell me, sir, then why does the ICMP need an exhumation and excavation division?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The role of the ICMP is to assist governments with addressing the problem of the missing and we provide assistance at the grave sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, we've got your CV. What, really, ability do you have to oversee such a unit?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I am, in that regard, a scientific manager and I rely on our staff to provide the true expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So do you often go to the field or do you ever go to the field?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I do not often go to the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just to clear that up then, basically some staff or staff members of the ICMP are the expert, not you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: In the specialisation of archaeology and anthropology, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 3 of the information sheet, supplemental information sheet which we had turned over to us on the 30th of January, 2008, you've indicated that the type of testing now used is nuclear STR typing; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't have the document that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You indicated in your earlier testimony that you had used previously to this a different type of testing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I wouldn't characterise it as a different type of testing, no. It would describe in terms of the general categorisation of type as the same. There was an instrumentations switch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So is your testimony then the ICMP has always utilised nuclear STR typing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, isn't it a fact, sir, that the term "nuclear" implies that it is not mitochondrial DNA that is being used?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And doesn't this fly in the face of almost every other lab -- what every other lab is doing for DNA testing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree, sir, that there is an enormous body of literature indicating that nuclear DNA cannot be successfully extracted from decomposed material including bone?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Absolutely untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Further, would you agree that in order to establish identity with nuclear DNA, a number of relatives one generation removed is necessary, for example, ideally you would want both parents to identify a child; et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That is not always the case, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But is it normally the case?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: If you have a mother and a father, for example, you're very, very strong grounds to make an identification. You can make identifications on any number of relatives depending on their combination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, you said that it's not normally the case. In what percentage would you give us that is the case?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: It depends on what family members are involved and what the genetic type of the individuals are; so there's not really a way to give an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And it's my understanding that the ICMP is claiming that you can identify individuals using samples from relatives such as uncles, aunts, second cousins and even spouses by using this nuclear DNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: It is a scientific fact that those types of individuals can be useful in making identifications. I would sincerely doubt that ever reached a statistical threshold on any one of those given relatives that you just mentioned has been achieved at the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, did the ICMP ever use or utilise MT DNA identifications?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Not in-house, no. Essentially no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, also with this type of DNA testing that you're using and that we're talking about, the nuclear STR typing, isn't it a fact, sir, that -- and won't you agree with me that what you need to make a claim valid would be a DNA sample obtained in life from the purported victim?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And are you saying then that doing nuclear DNA identifications with distant relatives is not speculative?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I am saying that, yes. I'm saying it's quite well-established in the field in many different applications that very strong evidence for identity can be obtained using relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, on page 3 you made a statement, and I could read it to you, it says that when samples arrive for testing, the ICMP does not work off the information accompanying them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It's on page 3 of the -- sir, I could hand this to you real quickly. I can read it to you. This is what -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can I put this on the ELMO real quick. And while we're doing that for the record this is a three page -- or four-page supplemental information sheet provided by Mr. Vanderpuye for the Office of the Prosecutor indicating this witness was contacted by telephone on 24 December 2007, again 24 January 2008, and there's some additional information given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Parsons is that correct? Did you talk to Mr. Vanderpuye on those two dates?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I -- I can't -- I can't attest to -- to what date that I would have spoken to him, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't doubt that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you see that where you told him that when samples arrive for testing, the ICMP does not work off the information accompanying them?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't see that. Can you direct me more specifically to the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Second to last point on that page. You have to move it up.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: You have to scoot it up, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, that would have been a -- as near as I can tell, this is not a statement that -- that I personally generated so this would look to me to be notes of Mr. Vanderpuye, and so I have to -- we have to understand what he might have been thinking in relation to what I had said. When the samples arrive for testing -- what I think that -- let me clarify what the ICMP does. When samples arrive to us from any number of sources, they are immediately entered into an anonymous -- anonymisation process so that the DNA typing is totally objectified throughout the entire process. We have no idea where the sample came from as it goes through the laboratory, who it might be, it could come from Kosovo, it could come from sure Hurricane Katrina victims, so that the end result of the matching is totally objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So I guess I should have asked you first, you didn't review the -- the supplemental information report before you came to testify today?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I have never - as far as I'm aware, I hope I'm not mistaken - seen this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. But it is true though that -- or it is not true that you did not work off the information accompanying them when the samples arrived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Materially I think the answer to that is it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: However, your protocols clearly outline a presumptive option; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, but that doesn't affect the samples that goes through the DNA laboratory. The knowledge of presumption does not occur in the laboratory processing system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's all I need that for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And so I would go to -- Your Honours, if we could have 65 ter 3174, the report of methodology 2001 to 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In looking at these, Doctor, and looking at the report that you had previously done from 2001 to 2006, in the standard operating procedures it looks like the majority are either original or earlier version of the SOPs you used; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Meek please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, you are giving your back to the microphone. And although I could hear you, the interpreters obviously couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that the SOPs, the majority of them were either original or earlier versions that were used by the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Are you talking about the methodology report 2001 and 2008?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Are they either original or earlier versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, on the first page of the standard operating procedure for silica-based DNA extraction from difficult skeletal remains and the amplification using Promega PowerPlex 16 system dated September 2003, are you familiar with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Not in any detail in terms of my ability to recall anything specific that would be written on that paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Well, we have -- are you familiar with silica-based DNA extractions, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How long have -- and it is used, is it not, for extraction of difficult skeletal remains?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: When did the ICMP begin utilising silica-based DNA extraction?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: 2002. Now, maybe you can clarify a few issues. On page 2, section 2 of the standard operating procedure again for the silica-based DNA, you explicitly discuss exhumed bodies; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't have that document in front of me. I can't answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that? Do you have a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Are you referring to the standard operating procedure itself or the -- or the methodology report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the standard operating procedure.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yeah. That's not what that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Standard operating procedure -- excuse me. 65 ter 3223. Yeah. I'm going to straight to that one. 3208. If we could have it pulled up. Now, if we could move to page 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Page 2, section 2, please. Do you see that, Doctor, under specimens? "The specimen is a human bone or tooth sample which is obtained from an exhumed body"?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you agree that surface deposits are almost always difficult or always included in the difficult extraction category?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You don't?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Are they sometimes or 50 per cent of the time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you speak into the microphone, please. Thank you. And the interpreters don't have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are they, sir, 50 per cent or more of the time included in the difficult extraction category? And I'm speaking of surface deposits.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I do not know the proportion that -- that would represent -- and there's no way to define something as difficult or not as an exclusive category so I don't know the ability to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, please put on your headphones, because intermittently the interpreters make requirements and you need to be alert to them. And the last one was that they do not have at their disposal this document. They have it now? Okay. Then slow down both of you, please, and speak into the microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You just testified, Doctor, that you don't really -- that the term "difficult" is hard to divine -- define. Is that what you said, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: In the context with which you posed the question, I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. But you just answered that the silica-based DNA extraction is used for difficult skeletal remains?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: We use it on all of our remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And is there any separate standard operating procedure for surface remains?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are they processed?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In the next paragraph you say the body must have been exhumed by trained professionals using standard operating procedures. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't know where that's written.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It may have been in your -- that may have been in the 2001, 2006, but is that a fact that the body has to be exhumed by trained professionals using standard operating procedures?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, it has nothing to do with DNA typing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No. Okay. But I'm talking about extraction of the body.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: We're referring to a DNA standard operating procedure here. If -- I mean, I could send a teenager out to exhume a body and they hand me the bone and I could do DNA typing on that bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't really need any trained professionals to dig up the bodies?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: It doesn't affect the results of the DNA test, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, in regards to field standard operating procedures, are you referring to Dr. Wright's reports from the ICTY, standard operating --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't know what field standard operating procedures you're talking about, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. As far as the exhumation of the bodies go, do you refer to anything that Dr. Wright or any of his reports?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't know who Dr. Wright is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay, now page 2, section 3 of the same document -- strike that question. In regards, sir, to the silica-based DNA extraction process, do you agree that the -- this modification that you made has shown to be more sensitive?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you explain to us, please, how the modifications have been tested to show the increased sensitivity? Has it been demonstrated?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, it has. Our techniques are formally validated with a comparison of previous extraction methodology to current extraction methodology. First of all, to show concordant results where the -- where the genetic information overlaps and also to demonstrate reproducibility of any additional genetic information that we may be obtaining from -- from the newly optimised technique and this has recently been published in the journal of forensic science international specifically with relation to this question. Also our formal experimental course of validation has been reviewed by our external accreditation agency and accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, has it been --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Has this been -- this testing been accredited you said by whom?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: One of -- one of the most significant international accreditation standards governing forensic DNA analysis is the standard of ISO 17025. And we have engaged a German company, the Deutsche Akkreditierungsstelle Chemie who is authorised via a number of international agreements to provide accreditation to the ISO 17025 standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, they have a web site and I looked on it and I couldn't find anywhere that the ICMP was accredited. In fact, they don't accredit forensic operations. So is it an individual that's accredited or --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The agency that I just referred to does accredit forensic operations; I would happen to know that because our agency is accredited by them and their web site does in fact list that we are accredited. I don't know how or where looked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That is DASH; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: DACH.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: DACH. Okay. Now, sometimes you have found that there have been low amounts of DNA that you can extract; correct? From bone samples --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, could you please speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Oftentimes you have a low amount of DNA that you can extract; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And what happens to the tests that are failed because you can't get enough DNA out of it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: What -- what we will do if we do not get a reliable DNA profile out of the bone very frequently is enquire if additional sample from the same specimen might be available where we could do another DNA extraction and hope that -- that the DNA preservation in another sampling is sufficient to yield a profile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Going back to DACH, why are you accredited by a German company rather than a US company or some other company since you are a US certified board?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I have no idea what you mean by us being a US certified board.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You -- I assume that you're a US based company; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You're not? Have you attempted to be accredited in any other places besides DACH?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, we have not. We -- we very carefully tried to determine one the most internationally respected accreditation agencies and that subscribes to the appropriate international agreements that would assure solid international recognition of the accreditation that we have and that is the reason we selected DACH.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And is it the fact that the calibrations on your machines are accredited or that your whole forensic lab was accredited?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The DNA laboratory system was accredited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay and not the individuals working there; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's correct. Well, there is not a separate accreditation for an individual. It's the laboratory that becomes accredited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And the laboratory would be the equipment, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No. It's the entire process. It's the SOPs, it's the people, it's the training processes. The oversight, the quality control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So would it be a fair statement that you are accredited for the methodology you use?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: It would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Rather than the lab facility itself?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No. Methodology is part of the laboratory process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. Some pauses, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How often, sir, if you know, would you undergo reaccreditation?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Our accreditation is valid through, I believe, 2012; but we undergo technical audits on annual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What is a technical audit?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Teams of experts from DACH and other forensic laboratories that they have engaged come in and witness the procedures that go on, refer to the documentation that we have and -- and do an in-depth audit of the methods that we use, the results that we obtain, and the processes that are involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Could we have 65 ter 3223 brought up, please. Dr. Parsons, while that's coming up, this is the -- the standard operating procedure for matching unit drafts. Could we look at page 2, point IV, IV, please. Now, it says in that paragraph -- it mentions a forensic expert; correct? Last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It says these DNA matching reports are reviewed for accuracy and then submitted to a forensic expert who can check the other information. Could you, sir, please give me a definition of how would you define a forensic expert and what are the minimum qualifications, education, experience in order to hold that title?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Our DNA match reports are submitted to court appointed forensic pathologists. They are the people that are authorised for us to turn that information over to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Could we move to page 5 of that document, point 11, please. What does that mean, briefly, when you say that it is compared using DNA rules?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: We're referring to number 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. Last sentence: "...and must be compared -- and must be written manually and compared using DNA rules." Do you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. In this case what that is referring to, they use -- they use a general statement about DNA rules. What they're referring to there is the pattern of heredity that occurs between different types of relatives. So in this case, for example, a mother, what the -- what the person in this screening process would be doing is ascertaining manually at this stage of the process that there is what is known as half allele share between the parent and putative offspring. That means that you get half of your DNA from your mother and half from your father; so at every genetic locus you're going to have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- at every genetic locus you will expect to find one shared allele.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, apparently you're using different queries for different --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Into the microphone, Mr. Meek, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Why are you using different queries for different situations?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: It's good question and it's a complicated process, but -- but there's a very good answer. In the end we only use one approach, but it depends on what reference one has what you're going to need to work through once you find a match. So if -- if you have just a mother and a sibling, for example, the initial screening software is going to indicate possible genetic relationships with one or both of those individuals, and it's this stage that this refers to. The person is -- is determining whether this candidate match is something to go on with or whether this match can be ruled out because it doesn't -- it doesn't follow the expected genetic relationships. If there is consistency, then they'll go on to the final stage where everything is the same and -- and that is where the genetic data is all brought into one central computer programme with a final statistic that is generated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have 65 ter 3225, which while it's being brought up is the SOP for DNA match report review. Page 2, point 1. Are you familiar with that, Doctor, or do you need to read it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I would need to take a quick can look at it. Of course I've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are you ready?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, could you explain when you say that the bone sample code assigned by the submitting pathologist, you see that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Does that include the skeletal element when they do that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Not in a systematic manner, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that the ICMP has nothing to do with manner or cause of death. It's not one of your duties or area of expertise?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't think that that's entirely accurate. It depends a little bit in the sense with which you ask it. Our anthropologists very frequently record data and information that's highly relevant to cause and manner of death, and our -- we have a forensic pathologist who we share with the clinical centre as a point -- court-appointed State pathologist, and he does rule as to cause and manner of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So you're saying that the ICMP does determine manner and cause of death in these remains that you work with?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: One of our employees in his capacity as a court-appointed pathologist does involve himself in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is he in house?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Is he in house?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is he an in-house expert?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: He is seconded to the ICMP. So he is stationed in one of our facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And what's his name, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Dr. Rifat Kasetovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What is his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I believe he is a Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: National. I should clarify though that the authority under which he performs that is not the authority of the ICMP. So -- and that's what I meant by saying it depends on the sense with which you ask that question. So possibly one of the best answers would have been, no, that's not our authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I have what, 12, 13 minutes left? If I'm only going to use 45 minutes out of the hour and a half?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know how much time you intended to use --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It was 45 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- but you have another 10, 13 minutes, proceed, conclude and then we have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I would like to take the break now, 10 minutes early, and then pare this down and get finished with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, that will create a problem for me because I have an appointment at 10.40.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Who pays this pathologist, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Both the ICMP and I believe the State of Bosnia. I know the ICMP does provide some salary; I can't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could we please have up 65 ter 3224, please. And while that's being brought up, Doctor, it's the standard operating procedure for -- called statistical calculation of DNA-based identifications using DNA view. Going to page 2, please. Section I. Now, are you familiar with that, sir, or do you need to read it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I would need to look at it. Maybe you could -- if you could ask the question and then I would see what --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] I'm sorry we're overlapping. The question I'm interested in would be five, six down, sentences, lines where it says: "Therefore a database of 424 individuals ..." Before we go further, sir, for the record, it didn't pick up the name of the pathologist. Could you say it slowly?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Last name is Kasetovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: First name?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Rifat. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is he a forensic pathologist?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is he board certified?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, again, back to 65 ter 3224. Don't you -- what's the source of this database first? We know that it comes from the ICTY; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. What's the source of it then?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: First of all, this is a database of anonymous individuals who have been typed genetically to determine the population frequency of the genetic elements that we look at to make the -- the calculations. So these are individuals not at all involved in the identification process. They're telling us about the population -- population genetics that we need to know in order to -- to do these calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, then how do you -- how do you know that these individuals represent the Bosnian population?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: They're randomly sampled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you know -- does your agency know the location of the residence, their birth, their ancestry?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, that's not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So it's all anonymous; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How do you know again? How do you know that they're from -- represent the Bosnian population?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: They're -- they're selected at random as -- I mean, there is a certain vetting process where the individual would be queried, where are you from, what is your ethnic background, and that would be used to include the selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What's the possible basis, sir, for knowing whether or not these individuals are unrelated to the potential victims? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, but not so much its relevance, but there would be no concrete evidence to suggest that -- that they couldn't be related to some victim. No reason to suppose that they would be either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It's just an assumption you're making, correct? And it's not based on any reasonable scientific basis.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I have no idea whether these people are related to a victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So again, you assume they're not.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't assume one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Well don't you agree with me, sir, that 424 as a base is inadequate, you should have more?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree, sir, that having more than 424 would strengthen your findings?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Do I not agree. That is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we need to go to the -- we had it up earlier. It's the letter from Dr. Parsons. I don't -- 65 -- we had it up earlier. 3005. Now, Doctor, you are familiar with this; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You're suggesting that the success rate of matching existing samples to family members is 95.7; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That would be 5.055 individuals out of the 5.280, correct, profiles you had?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You are, though, you'll agree, you're equating matching rates to collection rates for samples representing the missing; agreed?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Would you please say that again, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You're equating matching rates to collection rates for samples that represent the missing.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that phraseology is vague and I really sort of don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, sir, what's the basis for assuming that the samples collected so far are representative --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What is the basis for your assuming that the samples collected so far are representative in terms of a chance for a DNA match?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: What this document refers to is the sum total of material that we've dealt with in relation to Srebrenica, and -- and in -- in discussing this set of situations, we assume that the samples we've dealt with so far are typical of the chance for a DNA match, meaning, and I have no reason to believe that's not the case, meaning that there's not some small subset or -- or -- or set of remains that is -- is somehow missing in a way that would also cause us not to have any reference samples from it in a way that is different than all the rest of them. I'm sure that was -- I'm sure that that's a little bit hard for people to understand in the context of this discussion, but nevertheless it is the case, and I'm not aware of -- of any reasonable explanation why these would not be representative overall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So you're saying, then, that you have no reason to assume that all these individuals don't have an equal chance of being identified?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I'm saying I don't have any reason to believe that there is some small subset that has a different chance of being identified than the ones that we deal with here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, sir, to assume all individuals have equal chance, you would have to assume that they -- first, they have a grave containing their remains that's been found and exhumed; correct? B, that having at least one portion of the body survived that can be sampled. And third, having a successful DNA extraction; and lastly, having sufficient surviving family members to provide samples that you can match off of. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: All those conditions are required for a DNA match.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And isn't it unreasonable to assume that all this is going to happen?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I'm not assuming that all that's going to happening. I'm not even sure where you're going with that question or what the sense of the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that the -- the ICMP, when collecting DNA samples that all elements or body parts aren't sampled equally, that you get preference, for example, to body parts such as one long bone, leg bone?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes. We have a highly detailed sampling protocol that allows us the best chance for success.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, sir, further, don't your assumptions ignore the very real bias that's introduced by variable -- variables affecting the preservation and survival of the remains, including fire, decompensation and those things?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: You refer to my assumptions. I don't know what assumptions you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, the assumptions, sir, that the matching rates and the collection rates are going to be the same and they represent the missing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Your sentence has multiple components. The matching rates and the collection rates are going to be the same -- I don't know what that means. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. We can break it down. Explain to us, please, what is a matching rate in regard to collection rate?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: You would like me to explain the sense of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'd like you to explain the collection -- what are collection rates for samples as opposed to matching success?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The ICMP has a very active outreach programme to attempt to obtain genetic samples from family members of the missing. So far we have obtained genetic samples from family members who have reported missing individuals to us through this process relating to 7.772 individuals reported missing from Srebrenica. That is our collection. Those -- those are the samples we have collected. By the same token, the ICMP has obtained bone samples for DNA typing from 8.445 - as of November 30th - bone samples that relate to primary or secondary graves considered to be from the Srebrenica event. DNA has successfully been obtained from -- sorry, I misspoke. We have successfully obtained DNA profiles from -- for 8.445 such bone samples from Srebrenica. Some we were not able to obtain DNA from. Those represent 5.280 different individuals, meaning that some of the bone samples - because these are secondary graves that have been highly fragmented and commingled - some of the samples that have been submitted seperately actually refer to the same individual who has been dismembered. Okay? So as of the 5.280 profiles from different individuals that we have relating to Srebrenica, for those we have been able to match to family members 5.055. That gives us a matching rate -- in other words, if we take the total number of different profiles we've obtained, the matching rate and the overall process is about 96 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But the number of -- the number of DNA profiles is -- 5.280 is only 67 per cent of the total number of reported --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We need to get some -- you're saying, though, and I'm telling you I believe you say that you have DNA profiles of 5.280, and that's only 67.9 per cent of the total number of the reported missing individuals; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: There are 5.280 different individuals represented by the profiles, of which 5.055 have matched. When you divide 5.055 by 5.280, you get the value of 95.7 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But isn't there, sir -- you're saying -- you're not saying that there are allegedly 7.7 -- 7.772 reported individuals missing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: We have DNA samples representing 7.772 missing individuals from Srebrenica event. So you seem to be thinking that I'm claiming we've identified 95.7 per cent of these 7.772 individuals. It doesn't say that. I'm not suggesting that. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting is there's a fundamental flaw in your logic but I'm going to go on to -- to 2D176 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to break, Mr. Meek. Doctor, we'll have a 25-minute break and thank you for your patience and understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you finished, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Just a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Doctor, would agree with me that a DNA profile alone is not sufficient evidence of identification?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: As a basic statement, no, I would not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And would you agree that on several occasions the ICMP has argued for the need for anthropological examination as part of the DNA identification?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you're aware also that the ICMP and the ICTY cases have been criticised in a number of articles in regards to identification methods that you use?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Did you by any chance -- scan in 2D174, please, in e-court. This is an article --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: This is an article entitled, Erroneous gender identification by the Amelogenin sex test. Are you familiar with that article at all?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't have a specific recollection of having read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: On this Amelogenin sex test, do you use that in ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, that locus is one of the 16 loci that is typed in our process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you please scan in -- bring up in e-court 2D175. This will be an article entitled, What do the X and Y chromosomes tell us about sex in gender and forensic case analysis. Are you familiar with that, sir, that article?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: This one I believe that I have not read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please bring up on e-court 2D176? Entitled, The American Academy of Forensic Sciences, proceedings on the American Academy of Forensic Sciences. Have you -- and we're looking at page 2, H50. On the right side there. The importance of using traditional anthropological methods in DNA-led identification systems. Sir, are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You are familiar with that one?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And the author -- the authors of that did not criticise the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The authors of that are from the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. 2D177, please.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: May I request, please, to find out the year that this pertains to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I don't see the year off the top of my head but I can get it before you're finished testifying. 2005, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, it would be quite helpful for proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The copyright is 2005 on the front page. Second to last paragraph. Yeah. Could we please scan in --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: There's one that says 2003 on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's the next one. We don't need to go back to it unless you want to but the one previously that I just showed you, that was a copyright 2005, okay? Now, could we go to page 2, please.
