And under H20, the abstract of the influence of large scale DNA testing on the traditional anthropological approach to human identification: The experience in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are you familiar with that one, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No. I would have to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: One of the things they say, among other things, is that one misconception regarding DNA-led identifications is that once a DNA match is made, then a positive identification automatically follows. This is far from true. It is imperative that traditional forensic scientists review the tentatively identified remains and related evidence to ensure that the match is valid. Do you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Basically, yes. The word "imperative" might be a -- any given case is, in my opinion, an overstatement. And I would suspect - let me not speculate about anyone else - but I've not made any attempt to downgrade the importance of concordance of evidence between DNA and non-DNA. It's one of the pillars of our identification process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How many divisions do you have at the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that we call them exactly divisions, but I suspect the question you're asking is that we have three predominant parts of the forensic sciences division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How many employees do you have?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: In the forensics sciences department around a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Approximately, if you can tell me how many of those are ethnically Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that. I don't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One minute, Madam Tapuskovic. I reckon we have 29 minutes left. Is that correct? Please correct me if I am wrong. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, my name is Mira Tapuskovic and I'm one of the Defence counsel for Mr. Vujadin Popovic. In order to cut this examination of yours as short as possible, I hope you'll agree and that you won't hold it against me if I call the International Commission for the Missing Persons only commission for short, and I hope this won't be in the way of our communication.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's okay. Yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer out aloud so that it remains recorded in the transcript. You told us here that you applied standard operating procedures for DNA analysis. Can you tell me, were you the one to introduce the SOPs currently used by the commission?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who is it that issues these SOPs?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I believe the SOPs that were submitted have a listing as to who -- what's the word? -- who produced them. The SOPs that have been provided for the most part, to my knowledge, have a listing of the individuals who produced them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to know if the commission itself produced its SOPs or were the SOPs produced by some other body outside the commission, be it international organisations or any other type of organisation.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, almost by definition the standard operating procedure of a laboratory is that of the laboratory itself. It is simply a document that says precisely what is done. That isn't to say that the international commission on missing persons has invented all these DNA typing methods and in fact they are -- the fundamental science that they represent is extremely widely used around the world and publications and shared SOPs from other laboratories are widely used in the generation of -- of the SOPs that we have at the ICMP. So we take established techniques elsewhere that have been validated. We bring them in the laboratory. We test them. We validate them ourselves. We devise the way it works in our own hands, the way it works in our own facilities and that's what the SOP is. So the methods themselves are certainly not invented by the ICMP. In some cases, for example, our extraction methodology, before I arrived the scientists at the ICMP did experimentation and arrived at a very efficient mechanism for extracting DNA from bone. But in the main, these are established techniques.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. As you said, the extraction of DNA profiles is made pursuant to established procedures. In order for us to ascertain the appropriateness of a given DNA profile made, is it necessary for us to consult the electropherograms?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The electropherograms are the raw data by which an analyst derives the DNA profile. So -- but I don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question is if one would want to check the way in which the DNA profiling was made, does that person have to look at the electropherograms either for the DNA profiles made of bone samples or for the DNA profiles made from blood samples?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, in the sense that if I -- if I submitted a blood sample to a medical diagnostic laboratory and they gave me a result, I could say I don't know whether to trust that result until -- unless you send me all the raw data that gave rise to it. So if that's the sense you asked, then that's the case. On the other hand, I might -- I might refer to the fact that that is an accredited medical diagnostic laboratory and have faith that the result they reported is correct based on their established record.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please keep your answers short. My question was if one were to control the results, and I didn't go into who would be the controlling body. Does this mean that the control of the pherograms or the raw data as you put it can only be conducted by a professional?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you send to the OTP the electropherograms for 8.445 DNA profiles that you reference in your statement of the 31st of November --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- which is Exhibit 3005 in our case?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This means that none of the parties to the proceedings, neither the Defence or the OTP, are able to control the raw data.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The raw data has not been provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The standard procedures, are they produced in writing as a must?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The -- the scientific techniques that are used to produce a DNA profile don't depend on whether or not or in what form someone has written something on a piece of paper. What determines the outcome of a result is the methodology that goes into it, the actual physical experimentation that took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. An examination of the SOPs led us to conclude that there are some 40 of them. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I think that were provided to you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As we looked at the SOPs, we concluded that of 40 of them, 20 were produced in the second half of 2007. Three SOPs do not bear any date. Three SOPs date from 2006, and one from 2008. This is my question: Is the reason why the SOPs were produced in writing as late as they were, in 2007, connected with the accreditation that was sought from the German accreditation agency?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if this is -- counsel hasn't put to the witness what specific SOPs we're talking about because there were several more SOPs disclosed than are referred to in counsel's question. So I don't know that it's sufficiently clear what she's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if I should agree with you or not, but I think she put basically all the 40 but then reduced them to the first 20, then 3 and then 1. So I think it should be clear enough for the witness. Go -- please proceed, Madam Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We are pressed for time and that's why I did it this way. Thank you for understanding. I'm not sure if the witness answered. Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does every laboratory which is involved in forensic DNA analysis have the obligation to get an accreditation for its work from one of the internationally recognised accreditation agencies?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No. I would say there is no such general obligation. I believe in late 2006 or possibly early 2007, the forensic organisation ENFSI, the European Network for Forensic Science Institutes, did a survey of criminal DNA laboratories working in Europe and the answer was 70 per cent were not accredited.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the accreditation of a -- of a forensic laboratory for DNA profiling means, in essence, that at the international level it has been confirmed that the process of making DNA profiles in that particular laboratory seeking accreditation conforms with the international standard ISO 17025?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: If the laboratory is accredited to ISO 17025 standards then that is what the accreditation means, that it conforms with those standards.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us specify. ISO is a network of national institutions for standardisation; short?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't know that it is a network of institutions. I think it is an international standard of work that has been agreed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. This means that in the period between November 2001 when you started when DNA profiling, all the way through to the month of October 2007, that for the full six years during which your laboratory has been in existence you did not have that accreditation, that internationally recognised certificate?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: According to what we were able to conclude analysing all the documentation, the DNA profiling is a highly technical job of work, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In answer to my colleague's question, you said how many individuals were involved in DNA profiling. Can you tell me if there is an obligation -- or, rather, we do know there is an obligation for all the analysts to undergo the proficiency testing to verify their qualifications; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The word "obligation" is -- obliged by whom and under what standard? I'm unaware that there is some sort of universal obligation for proficiency testing. In fact, it is a quite useful tool in quality assurance.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us not waste time, but there are international groups that conduct proficiency testing of analysts every six months. Are you aware of the existence of such agencies?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I won't -- I don't know about the six months, but, yes, there certainly are proficiency testing operations. The one we use is called GEDNAP. It's a German agency that we perform our proficiency testing with.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do all your analysts undergo proficiency testings and do they get a passing mark?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The -- the GEDNAP programme tests the outcome of the laboratory; that is to say, the laboratory's ability to produce a genetic profile from submitted samples. So, again, it is not an individual by individual type of analysis. And we do participate in the GEDNAP trials and do obtain the certificates of the results, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The certificates your analysts received as well as the documentation given by the German accreditation agency, did you send those to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: They were not requested. The answer's no.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move on to a different topic since I don't have much time left. We received a document from the OTP, namely D0001516. That's for the benefit for the OTP. Where, and I will not be calling it up at this time, it is said that 649 persons were identified as a result of a classical or a classic method in the period since the inception of the commission in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was in 1996, and all the identifications were conducted through a classical method before DNA profiling was introduced in 2001. Can you confirm that -- whether these identifications were reidentified through DNA profiling or were they in fact not revisited at all?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't know the document you're referring to, and I don't know the 649 individuals you're referring to, nor do I know what role the ICMP played in any of the -- in the question that you discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The document that my learned friend from the OTP showed at the start of his examination-in-chief, that's 65 ter document 3002, the long list, can you confirm that these cases, no matter how many of them were in fact involved, these cases that were identified through the conventional methods, whether they were also included or in fact were not included on that list.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: On what list? I'm sorry, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we call up Exhibit 3002. And I believe it was 3002A, in fact.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Thank you. I now recognise the document. This is a list of DNA matches that were made. So I don't know anything about how this relates to any bodies that may or may not have been identified through non-DNA means. This is solely a list of DNA matches.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do your SOPs provide for the duplication or, rather, double-checks of DNA profiling?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes. There are a large number of double-checks. You used the word "duplication." I'll address that specifically. I suspect that you relate -- are referring to independent duplicate testing of the same samples, and up until late 2006, in every case possible, which was the vast majority, our bone samples were tested independently in duplicate with concordance as a -- as a basis for issuing the DNA match report. In late 2006, we did a large-scale quality control programme, because obviously it's very expensive to do these samples in duplicate, and we looked at many thousands of duplicate analyses, and with the result that there were no discrepancies between them, and we simply were no longer able to justify the cost-effectiveness of -- of this as a quality-control measure. So we now have criteria under which we do not duplicate. But for a vast majority of the samples on this list that we just referred to they were done independently in duplicate.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This means that you're departing from the SOP which is currently in force in the commission, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't know the basis for your statement of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the standard procedure governing --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: We instituted a new policy and a new SOP based on the quality-control analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one question left. My colleague put quite a few questions concerning document 3005, which is your statement of November 2007. I will read this one sentence out to you: [In English] "To date ICMP has received reference samples relating to 7.772 individuals reported to be missing in July 1995." [Interpretation] If my understanding is correct, Mr. Parsons, we don't know how many reference samples you have here, but we do know that 7.772 individuals were reported to be missing. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, I'd love to have the document up here just to be correct, but that is correct. For 7.772 individuals, family members have reported them missing to us and provided at least one blood sample relating to that individual, relating to Srebrenica, or according to those family members.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Parsons, that for that statistical operation where you calculated that there was a possibility that the total number of the missing persons was 8.100, you factored in the -- not the DNA profiling results but, rather, the number of persons who had been reported as missing, which in fact is a figure that has not been confirmed yet and is a hypothetical factor?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: There is nothing hypothetical about the fact that -- that people gave us blood samples referring to 7.772 missing loved ones. It's a simple statement of fact that that's what we have, and that's what my document refers to.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in this document you did not state the number of reference samples, did you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No. No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Nikolic, there are only three minutes to four minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I apply for an extension of 10 minutes since my colleague overstepped the time that we agreed upon yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You should have seen it and stood up when your colleague was doing precisely that, not now. In any case, I will consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few questions only. Good morning, Mr. Parsons. My name is Jelena Nikolic, and I appear on behalf of Mr. Drago Nikolic. Does the ICMP issue death certificates?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Who is in charge of issuing those?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Court-appointed medical pathologists.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It means that the ICMP establishes neither the year nor the manner and time of death?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. An agreement was concluded between the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and your institute at the moment of its inception. In Article 4, it mentions cooperation with the relevant organisations, including this Tribunal -- or, rather, the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I'd have to refer to the agreement. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could we please bring up 3D293 in e-court, and just to save some time we can place the hard copy on the ELMO. The first and the last page, please. Particularly I'm interested in the third page of the document, Article 4. In bullet point 3 is what I referred to, and I believe I highlighted that in your copy. Can you answer my question now?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I would be delighted to. You have to remember that I am a scientist and this -- this area is -- of government agreements, et cetera, is simply not where my professional life intersects. So under bullet point 3 it says: "Cooperates with relevant authorities." I don't know what this refers to, so I would have to look at this entire document to assess what we're dealing with here. Signatory parties -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm merely interested in the cooperation with the OTP of this Tribunal. Do you have standing correspondence in cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor pursuant to this agreement?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: When you -- when you add the phrase "pursuant to this agreement," I'm going to have to decline to answer unless I review it in great detail and understand more about it. If you want to ask what interactions we've had with the OTP, I would be happy to answer those questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would kindly ask you to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: And I'm very sorry, could you please repeat it just one more time now that we're at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is the nature of interaction and communication between you and the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, it varies under different circumstances, but the work that we do is conducted wholly independently of the Office of the Prosecutor, but apparently they conclude that some of the -- some of the work that we do is relevant to the proceedings of this Tribunal, and therefore they have requested from us information that we have as a result of our work to return the missing persons to their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In September 2007, did you ask for financial support for your institute through the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes. It's a very big problem. As I mentioned before, we're involved in -- in returning missing people to their families, and some of the requests that the Prosecutors have made in terms of information because it doesn't relate to our core mission, put an extreme extra burden on us from the standpoint of providing materials, and that is not how we are funded. So the point that we've made is that we require some type of extra funding to -- to cover the activities that we have here, simply because any resources that we apply then specific to a request for information detract from our core mission of the work that we do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you turned to the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Tribunal in The Hague for that assistance on the 28th of September, 2007.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't have any documentation of that. I can confirm that we -- that we said -- that we indicated that funding would be welcome. I can also confirm that none has ever been forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask that this document be not broadcast. It is 3D296 in e-court, and there is a hard copy for the witness. Please read the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Aloud, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. No, for your information. I'm trying to assist you in order to be able to answer my question. My question was whether you turned to the Office of the Prosecutor for assistance on the 20th of November, 2007.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Who is this letter from?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: And who is it addressed to?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can scroll down and then you'll see the signature block.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I see a letterhead, but I need some grounding on what we're looking at here. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please take the document. Read the first paragraph in which the Office of the Prosecutor, pursuant to your request, turned to some donors for financial assistance. That is all.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm looking at this. It appears to be a letter from Vice-president Franco Frattini from the European Commission; is that correct? I'm asking you for assistance here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it it's the inverse. It's the opposite, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, and we also have some concerns that the document might be Rule 70, which we discussed with counsel before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if you have concerns, you better check before it becomes too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The other objection is to the extent that the witness has already conceded that the ICMP has made a request of the Office of the Prosecutor with respect to funding, I don't see the relevance of this line of questioning. I would ask that counsel move on to a different point or make the question more germane to the issues at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Do you wish to comment on that, Ms. Nikolic, or do you wish to proceed with your next question?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I believe the witness did not answer, and he asked for the document in order to be able to do so. If he answered, I agree with my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It was an issue of the date. Counsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It involves many issues, Mr. Vanderpuye, including the relevance of the whole line of questions that we have had throughout this sitting today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned friend had put the question to the witness as to whether he was aware that such a request was made on a specific day in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let the witness answer the question if he can. Can you answer the question, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would request, please, just for it to be posed simply one more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you put the question, please, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, did your institute turn to the Office of the Prosecutor asking for assistance in order for them to support your request for further financial institution from certain donors.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In September 2007?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Again we'd have to get into documents. This is not an area of my professional interaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I won't insist on the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: One additional question only. When gathering information on your institute, on its web site inter alia it is stated that one of the tasks is to assist international tribunals and domestic courts in order to help resolve events that have to do with war crimes and crimes against humanity as well as genocides and -- genocide and other crimes in contravention of the international law.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Is there a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, you stated a fact about our web site. Do you have a question about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Is one of the roles of your institute to establish whether genocide happened since this is what I found on the web page of your organisation.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, it is not one of the roles of our institute to determine whether genocide has been accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Why is that on your web site then?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I would have to refer to the web site. Your wording seems unfamiliar to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could we please bring up 3D295A and B in e-court, and I will conclude my cross-examination thereafter. 3D295A and B in e-court, and I have a hard copy with the relevant portion highlighted for the witness. A is the English version, page 2, and page is the B/C/S version. Please have a look at page 2, sir. I underlined the penultimate paragraph. It begins with the word: "[In English] ICMP has also provided support ..."

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I was correct. The wording here was substantially different than that you posed to me earlier. What it says is: "The ICMP has also provided support to international and domestic courts on matters related to war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide, and other crimes under international law in line with data protection and other safeguards under ICMP policy." What that would refer to, I think, that you would like me to tell you is providing the type of information that we did provide here as evidenced by -- by this list insofar as these -- such undertakings find interest in the work that we do in terms of providing identifications and -- and -- to the family members.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it there is no re-examination, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, we've finished your testimony. I can't thank you enough for having come over. I know how busy a man you are. Thank you, and on behalf of everyone, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are there documents that either of the parties seek to tender in relation to this witness? Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, there are. Your Honour, I would like to offer basically everything that's in the exhibit list. There is -- there are a couple of exceptions. One is 65 ter 3003B. One is 65 ter 3004. And that's all. So other than those documents, everything that's on the exhibit list I would tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections? Yes. These are admitted. Madam Registrar, you need to take -- make sure that those that are indicated as -- to be preserved under seal are kept so, okay? Mr. Meek, do you wish to tender any documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. 2D174, 2D175, 2D176, and 2D177.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections from either the Prosecution or the other Defence teams? Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There's no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So these four documents are admitted. Madam Tapuskovic, would you like to tender any document?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Popovic Defence seeks to tender no documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. First I'd like to thank you for the additional time you gave me, and we used three documents. These are 3D293, 3D295A and B, and 3D296. I believe the list had been forwarded. And the last document is confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You also had to check -- thank you, Madam Nikolic, whether one of the documents used by Madam Nikolic is covered by Rule 70 protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct what?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That we do have to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My understanding is that it is actually indicated in that way. The other thing is I would object to it on the basis of relevance since the witness clearly had no familiarity with it and couldn't even attest to the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can expect all sorts of submissions in due course, so leave it there for the time being and we'll see. We'll see later. So that concludes -- they are admitted these three documents. That concludes the testimony of Dr. Parsons. Let's get back to Mr. Butler. Mr. McCloskey. Is Mr. Butler here? All right. One moment, because there is a preference here to hear the submissions on the two motions that I referred to yesterday before we proceed with the testimony of Mr. Vanderpuye -- of Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The reason I rose is if the Court recalls, I had been granted leave to ask Mr. Butler two minutes' worth of questions but I'll do that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is -- was agreed upon yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed. It was indicated to me yesterday evening, and I'm grateful to Your Honours' senior legal officer for his cooperation and assistance, that the Trial Chamber did want to hear our submissions in relation to the motion seeking to add one witness to the list and as a result I'm in a position to address the Chamber. I'm bound to say in passing that whilst I understand the Chamber's desire for expedition in this matter, we do make the submissions to some extent under protest, bearing in mind the time involved, but turning to the substance of the matter, Your Honours, we strongly oppose the motion of the Prosecution. As a preliminary, perhaps I could deal with paragraph 4 of the motion. Could I have just one moment. And in particular, I make reference to the fact that Mr. McCloskey, in effect, emphasised that paragraph yesterday in his brief reply to what I had to say. We wish the Trial Chamber to be clear that any suggestion that the Defence brought this situation upon ourselves is totally rejected and is completely unfair. As has been recognised and accepted by the Prosecution, General Smith first mentioned this particular issue to the Prosecution in late October of last year during a proofing session. The Defence sought, by way of an oral motion on the 1st of November of last year, in effect an order preventing the Prosecution leading that evidence. The Trial Chamber rejected that oral submission. Thereafter, Smith gave the evidence. Of course the Defence were then confronted with the evidence, and we put our case, as is my habit, forcefully to him. At that time there was not a jot of evidence to support what he was saying, and no doubt had there been I would have been stopped in the questions that I had asked. I wasn't misleading, being unfair, or in any way misrepresenting the position. I also did, I would venture to suggest, what any prudent counsel would do in that situation and that is test the evidence that we faced at that particular time. The comment in paragraph 9 of this motion that the fact -- is unfair because at the time the corroborative evidence did not exist and as I've already said, the cross-examination was unobjectionable. Turning, if I may, to paragraphs five and six of the motion, the Defence note with some interest the "sustained efforts" of the United Kingdom authorities to find this particular witness. Sadly, those sustained efforts don't appear to have got very far. But as I said yesterday, I will make a submission about whether the Prosecution to some extent have brought this upon themselves and whether they've acted within -- with all due expedition. We make no criticism of what they have done over the last few months in relation to time, but we would observe that if anyone had bothered to interview Smith properly in the first place about his dealings with Gvero, then this allegation would have emerged months if not years ago. The fact of the matter is clearly no one asked him any proper questions about what dealings Smith had with Gvero until Mr. Thayer went to see him in late October of last year. And to a large extent we suggest that it's, frankly, bad investigation. And whether the fault lies with the lawyers or the investigators doesn't matter; for this purpose we lump the Prosecution together. It's bad prosecuting that has made this happen because, of course, had the allegation that Smith makes been made to the Prosecutors at an earlier stage, they clearly would have followed up the trail and the Defence wouldn't have been left in this highly prejudicial position of having to meet the evidence not just in the middle of the trial but virtually at the end of the Prosecution case. It certainly isn't the Defence fault, and we do ask the Trial Chamber to ask yourselves whether perhaps some fault does lie at the door of the Prosecution. Your Honour, the arguments advanced by the Prosecution in paragraph 11 of this motion are greatly depreciated by the Defence. The conversations that are alluded to in this motion were not written. We suggest they were, in effect, counsel-to-counsel conversations, and the propriety for including them in this motion is dubious in the extreme. The end result of including that type of counsel-to-counsel negotiation in a motion like this is a complete breakdown of communication between the parties. Why should we have anything to do with Prosecutors who throw this sort of information back in our face? That being said, I don't want to suggest for one moment that what is contained in here is untrue. It's there. You've seen it. There's no point in me resigning from it. It is true and I want to make that clear. And we stand by our actions in the matter and perhaps I could make a number of submission that is flow from that. After the conversations that are described in paragraph 11, the Prosecution at no point returned to the Defence and said what they were doing and in particular that they had located this particular witness. In other words, they didn't say, "We've located the witness. We're now going to see her. Do you now want to be involved in the process?" In short, they happily parade what we did back last year, but they don't keep the Defence up-to-date, and I simply mention that in the context of them relying on the information in paragraph 11. Next, Your Honour, the Prosecution end that paragraph by saying that no injury or prejudice will be suffered by the accused as a result of our own actions. We suggest that is a total non sequitur. In short, we don't follow that submission whatsoever. Why as a result of our decision last year no injury or prejudice is caused to our client is beyond our comprehension and perhaps the Prosecution will enlighten the Court about that in due course. The fact that prejudice matters the Prosecution concede at the beginning of this motion in paragraph 4 where they say the addition would cause no prejudice to the accused. So the question of prejudice matters. As I mentioned yesterday, the issue of prejudice, which Mr. McCloskey so lightly tossed away and said we all know the law on it - we're all experts on it, apparently - is not something we had a chance to research, is something we would like to have researched and is something we would like to have addressed. Prejudice in the general sense and also prejudice specifically as to a witness of this sort being raised at this juncture of the case. I'm not in a position to advance any law in relation to matter for reasons I have just explained, but we would suggest that our client is greatly prejudiced and the Prosecution's suggestion that as a result of our actions described in paragraph 11 that he's not is simply wrong. Returning finally so far as paragraph 11 is concerned to my third point, most importantly of all the Defence make a tactical decision as described in paragraph 11. We stand by that tactical decision. In the course of any case, particularly a long criminal case like this, the parties have to make difficult tactical decisions from time to time. Those decisions are of course based on judgement, common sense, but above all else the law, the rules, and the procedure, and I will develop that, if I may, in a few moments' time when I come to end my submission. One small but important matter we mention in passing, appendix A of this motion sets out what this witness purports to say. Interestingly itself falls foul of Rule 65 ter (E)(ii)(c) because it does not particularise which parts of indictment this will go to and we would ask for such particularisation in due course. Your Honour, moving on from this point, if the Trial Chamber grant this application, the Defence do require more time to prepare for the cross-examination of this particular witness. We require and submit we're entitled to the 30 days' notice that has been acceded to and granted to every other defendant in this case in relation to every other witness who's given evidence in this case and in relation to this witness the position should be no different. We are aware, of course, of your decision of a week ago, the 25th of January in relation to the last such Prosecution application. Excuse me. Where at, I think, page 20501 Your Honour, the learned Presiding Judge, mentioned the possibility of the witness being discussed on that occasion being called in rebuttal. This is not the moment for me to rehearse or make submissions in relation to rebuttal evidence in this Tribunal, but we would respectfully suggest that the test for rebuttal is not made out in such circumstances, and leaving aside that witness, because that witness is neither here nor there as far as this application is concerned and certainly has no bearing on our case, we would invite the Trial Chamber to consider very carefully whether any such similar ruling could possibly be made in relation to this witness. I was looking, because I have a brief synopsis of the law of rebuttal in the Tribunal. As I say, perhaps now is not the time to even quote that but I would submit to the Court that that simply isn't an answer to this particular motion. Moving on if I may, yesterday Your Honour suggested the ability of a Trial Chamber to call a witness itself. Well, of course that exists clearly under the rules. There is no question so far as that is concerned, but broadly speaking, we would submit that similar considerations would have to apply there, particularly where it's known that one of the parties is very anxious, indeed desperate to call that witness, and the other party is suggesting that that witness should not be called. And in those circumstances, realistically, to say that that witness should wait to the end and be called as a Chamber witness by reason perhaps of either scheduling or other considerations is simply unfair and not a proper way to proceed. The rules of this Tribunal are basically that the Prosecution put up a case. The Defence then meet it if they see fit. In short, we submit this is ostensibly an adversarial process, rightly or wrongly. Most importantly of all, as I have already said, the Defence are entitled to rely on the Rules of Procedure of the Tribunal and are entitled to expect decisions that flow from those rules. In conclusion, I ask rhetorically, what does that amount to in this case? In other words, reliance on the Rules of Procedure. We submit as follows: If the Trial Chamber feel that this witness should be called, she should be called as part of the Prosecution case or not at all. In short, it's now or never. Now, I've already made submissions as to why we say she shouldn't be called at all and we're prejudiced, and I've already said I would have liked to have developed that a bit further, but be that as it may we submit it's now or never. However, it's not right now we submit. We submit that we're entitled to prepare for her in the way that everyone else has been entitled to prepare for other witnesses before she gives evidence. And so she should be called, I say she should be called before the end of the Prosecution case and allowing the Defence proper time to prepare prior to her evidence. Thereafter, the Defence can state categorically that in the event that this lady does give evidence, there will be an application for the recall of three or four Prosecution witnesses who gave important evidence on this topic prior to Smith making his allegation; in other words, before anyone was aware that this was going to become a live and important issue in this case, and certainly the three of those witnesses would be Joseph, Dibb, and Savcic. We recall Your Honour's words on the 2nd of November of last year when Your Honour ruled on our original application at page 1 -- 17.408 of the transcript where Your Honour said that the Court would listen to any ad hoc application from the Defence. Again, we chose, let me make no bones about it, made a tactical decision not to make that application after Smith gave his evidence, but our decision will be completely different, I can categorically state, in the event of this lady giving evidence. It changes the situation radically as far as we are concerned. And, Your Honour, I'll end, if I may, by saying what I stated yesterday. If what I'm saying on behalf of General Gvero has a radical effect on the schedule of this trial, then let's be clear, that is not down to General Gvero or his lawyers. We have not brought this situation upon ourselves. We didn't ask for this application to be made. I know it's an obvious point. And we would like to adhere to the present schedule as much as possible; but we do submit that if justice demands that this witness be called and that's the consideration of the Trial Chamber, then scheduling constraints must not get in the way of things being done in a proper and just manner. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon everyone. I will just address a couple of the issues. I won't address all of the comments my friend made. I'll just begin by starting with his discussion of the discussions that he and I had after General Smith's testimony and I'll be brief on this issue. I don't see anything untoward in including these discussions in our motion. I think this goes in the category of no good deed goes unpunished. We had no obligation to consult with my friends with respect to how we were going to proceed in following up this information that General Smith disclosed at such a late date. We would have just gone out and, as we frequently do, follow up on information by ourselves with no input from Defence counsel. Given the unique situation that we were facing with this information coming up in the middle of trial, I thought it was only fair to invite my friend to be party to any of these follow-up discussions either in person, if it was by telephone by telephone, or even to submit questions. I didn't have to do that. I did it. In any event. His answer was equivocal after some consideration. No. Do what you have to do and we will hear from you one way or another. I don't see any and I did not see any need to follow up. I thought his answer was what it was. I took him at his word that that was his considered decision. As he said, it was a tactical decision and he should live by it. I don't think there's anything improper in letting the Court know where the parties stood with respect to these events. In fact I think it's important for the Court to understand the overall context and how this information has been has developed. Now, I appreciate that these developments are unwelcome for the Gvero team, but as everyone knows, they emerged naturally from this information which General Smith disclosed. All the parties were taken by surprise. The Court has already ruled with respect to General Smith's testimony on this issue that it was interested in hearing this. That is our understanding of the Court's ruling. This was information that was relevant and probative. And my friend at that time when he made his arguments trying to exclude the testimony, proffered no basis in fact or law as to why that testimony should have been excluded, and he has not today either. This is very simple testimony which we have seen the possibility of coming for some time now. My friend was obviously adequately prepared to cross General Smith on this issue at the time. He did so. I don't see any reason why he can't be similarly and adequately prepared to cross-examine this proposed witness immediately. She is available next week. She is holding open dates for the Trial Chamber on which she is able to appear. This is not a surprise in any respect with respect to how the Prosecution has argued General Gvero's position, his culpability. This testimony goes directly to counts 6, persecutions, with respect to the forceful transport -- forcible transfer, deportations; counts 8 -- or 7, the forcible transfer; and ultimately count 8, the deportations with respect to the Zepa enclave. This information, as we've argued previously, is perfectly consistent with all the testimony this Court has heard of General Gvero's hands-on activities from his presence at Pribicevac to his 12 and 13 July orders, to all of the documents and orders concerning Zepa and the negotiations that General Gvero was copied on to his involvement in setting up the 25 July meeting between General Smith and General Mladic specifically to resolve the Zepa situation, to his 31 July meeting in Mrkonjic Grad with General Mladic at which resolving the issue of Zepa, again, was on the agenda. It shows clearly and consistently General Gvero's active participation throughout the entire time period charged in the indictment and in particular with respect to these forcible transfer charges. It shows how he was active and he supported General Mladic all the way to the end. We even have General Skrbic talking about how at this time at the end of the July General Gvero is at the front line dodging bullets. That is absolutely consistent with the Prosecution's theory. The proposed testimony from this proposed witness fits perfectly in that. General Gvero is on site, on site in Zepa as he was in Srebrenica at Pribicevac. This corroborates what General Smith testified to. My friend asked for corroboration. He now has it. The Court, I believe, should hear it. This is evidence which is relevant, probative, and can and ought to be heard now, not later. There is no reason advanced by my friend why he can't be prepared to cross-examine this witness. With respect to other witnesses that he cares to, as he says, do investigation on, he has the information report from Tom Dibb who we interviewed. As for General Skrbic or Ed Joseph, they can be called in the Defence case. I don't see how, in any event, that affects his ability to cross-examine this witness that we've proposed. And again we're happy to make arrangements at any time, as we were before, for my friend to interview anybody that we have previously called but that's beside the point. The issue is why he is not in a position to cross-examine this witness on a very limited issue, what she saw when she was at that check point and encountered General Gvero at Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Josse very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. We wish to carry out further investigation. We wish to speak to a number of witnesses. Could I make it absolutely clear that any suggestion that we should have a call those witnesses who gave evidence in the Prosecution case as part of our Defence case is totally rejected. That would be shifting the burden of proof, and we would say that the Trial Chamber shouldn't countenance that for one moment. The prejudice there is quite obvious. We would have asked these questions of those witnesses had we known of the allegation at the time they gave their evidence. So that has nothing to do with the time we require. We require time for further investigation. We'd also ask for those witnesses to come back and for us to be allowed to cross-examine them, not call them as our own witnesses. I hope that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. That's clear, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, could I just -- one point of information, general Skrbic, by the way - and we can actually point to the evidence - General Skrbic did sort of say my client was dodging the bullets. He was dodging the bullets in the Krajina on the 27th of July according to General Skrbic. I mention that in passing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to have the break now. We are going to discuss this and come to a conclusion possibly, and then of course we will come to the other matters. I think we better earmark a 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just want to know if you wish to hear any submissions regarding the Prosecution motion on 92 quater after the break or after the testimony of Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I know you want to take the break. Just regarding the 92 quater, I'm prepared to argue that today, however, my suggestion would be that this just be dealt with on paper and that the Defence file a response perhaps by Monday. We filed our motion Tuesday and they've been on notice of this for months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We would have given Mr. Josse the same treatment if that would have been our choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just find there is less urgency regarding this motion perhaps than the question of calling another witness. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There's a lot of urgency, Mr. Nicholls, because the Prosecution case is coming to an end and we are handing down a decision today establishing that deadline again, or extending the current deadline from today to whenever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we certainly do not intend to address the merits of the motion but the consequences thereof is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. We do not underestimate the import.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Anyone who has been following the proceedings today would certainly, I hope, have dispelled any ideas they might have as to whether we work hard and under what conditions we work sometimes. Once more thank you, Mr. Josse and Mr. Thayer for your submissions and for making them within a reasonable time. We are going to decide the Prosecution motion to add the witness to whom we have referred -- which is referred to in the motion. We are seized of this motion to add her to the 65 ter list and to have her appear to testify before the close of the Prosecution case. We have heard oral submissions on the issue from the Gvero Defence team and the reply of the Prosecution to that. The issue which the witness will testify to is clearly relevant and probative. The only question is that of prejudice. We do not accept the general arguments of the Gvero Defence team that prejudice would result from hearing this witness at this stage given the history of the matter and in particular the late disclosure of this particular piece of evidence by General Smith. That point was already ruled upon by the Trial Chamber in its earlier decision to reject the Defence motion to prevent General Smith from testifying on the matter. The only question in our mind is whether hearing the evidence in the short time remaining before the close of the Prosecution case will prejudice the Defence of General Gvero because of a lack of time to prepare for the cross-examination of this witness. We note in this regard that the Gvero Defence has expressly indicated its preference to have the witness called at this stage as part of the Prosecution case as opposed to later as a Trial Chamber witness. On the question of prejudice, the evidence of the witness goes to an extremely limited though important point regarding an encounter with General Gvero. We cannot in these circumstances see the need for an extensive period of time for the preparation of the cross-examination. In particular, we note that in relation to General Smith, the Defence of General Gvero facing similar if not more limited time constraints was able to mount a thorough cross-examination of him on this point. In order to grant as much time as possible to the Defence of General Gvero, we are hereby ordering that the witness be the last of the Prosecution witnesses who will be called. However, as is evident from what I have been stating so far, we are granting the Prosecution motion to add the witness to the 65 ter list and call her to give evidence. As to the question of recalling other Prosecution witnesses to be cross-examined on this issue and limitedly on this issue, we agree with the Gvero Defence that it would not be appropriate to force them to be called as part of the Defence case. Therefore, in light of scheduling issues, if the Defence of General Gvero wish to recall these witnesses for cross-examination, on this limited point, they will be permitted to do so prior to the opening of the Gvero Defence case as part of a technical reopening of the Prosecution case. And this is of course subject to the decision pursuant to Rule 98, depending, in other words, on whether we decide ultimately that the case against General Gvero should proceed as is or limitedly. So that's our decision. Yes. Thank you Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour, and I don't want to be obstructive here. I'll need to discuss that, of course, with my client and Mr. Krgovic, and we will need to decide whether we're going to seek certification of that decision. If we're going to do that, how should that practically be done, in writing or orally, first session? Thinking aloud, I would invite the Trial Chamber to allow us to make that application orally at the first sitting of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is granted. Thank you. When I say that is granted, we are not granting --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand. And I emphasise the word "if".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. Okay. Mr. Bourgon, you wish to address the Chamber on the other motion on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. We would like to make some submissions on behalf of the accused that we represent, Drago Nikolic, concerning the Prosecution motion to have admitted in evidence four witnesses pursuant to Rule 92 quater. May we go into private session, Mr. President, for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Bourgon. Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. If you would kindly proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The situation regarding the Prosecution 92 quater motion is quite different from the arguments which you have heard on behalf of my colleague representing the accused Gvero. Our submission addresses two issues. The first issue being the time required to respond to the motion on the merits, and the second issue being the consequences of having this motion filed at this time. Mr. President, regarding the first issue, which is the time required to respond, we will require a significant amount of time to respond to this motion for the following reasons: One, the motion deals with a complicated area of the law, namely addition into evidence of statements of persons who are no longer available and in this case persons who are deceased. Responding to this motion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, let me interrupt you for a moment to give you advanced notice of a decision that we have already taken in respect to this motion, a decision which does not go to the merits, a decision which is basically the following: We've decided that this motion of the Prosecution, precisely because of the short time available for the Defence teams to be prepared for it, to come forward with their position, should not and will not be decided prior to the exercise and the decision that we will be reaching pursuant to Rule 98. Bis, yes. So the position that the Trial Chamber is going to take is that for the purposes of the Rule 98 bis process, your submissions, in particular, you are to take it for granted that the testimony of these four persons do not exist in the record and will not form part of the record. In other words, the Rule 98 bis decision will be taken irrespective and independently of the testimony of these four persons. Subsequently, after we have handed down the Rule 98 bis decision, which will articulate whether the case will proceed against all accused or -- or as is or against some of the accused, we will be handing down the decision in relation to this motion, and after, of course, having had -- after having given you the opportunity to come forward with your responses. So that is our decision. In other words, these -- the testimony of these four persons will not be taken into account for the purpose of the Rule 98 bis decision, and you're free to make any other comments you like which are relevant to what could be usefully discussed this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. This is very useful. We take good note. We will respond to this motion in the time allotted to us pursuant to the Rules. However, there is one -- the rest of our arguments will be put into our response, but just to -- as an advance notice, this motion may very well imply that if it was to be granted in respect of Witness 102, there are additional witnesses that we would like to call for further cross-examination, and these witnesses are those that we have highlighted earlier on in a similar motion in respect of Witness PW-108. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours and thank you for your guidance on the motion. We join obviously in the objection and will isolate it for the Court particularly which witness or witnesses we think go against Mr. Beara. We believe though that because we talked a little bit about prejudice and that the Prosecution's position seems to be simple and straightforward that nothing causes prejudice to the accused. And I think my learned friend has suggested that there's no case law on it or that it's pretty clear the case law. That shouldn't be his position. It's unfortunate that they use that tactic that nothing causes prejudice. This motion violates not only this Court's Rules that you've set in proceedings during this trial but also the Rules of Evidence of this Tribunal, and I have to raise this as one issue because it will be highlighted in our brief, we hope, and that is that the witnesses that have been deceased since -- that they're seeking application pursuant to 92 quater, they've known that these witnesses have passed away, and they've known for some time after the proceedings in this case started that these people were either sick or potentially could become deceased. They've done nothing and sat on their hands. For them to suggest that they have -- that the Defence somehow knew about this motion for some time really is not the question that the Court should ask, and the real question is why didn't the Prosecution in the beginning of their case when these individuals were alive, at least a couple of them, why didn't they call those individuals early in the case as opposed to wait until the very end of their case to try to make an application pursuant to a new amended Rule 92 quater? I think that's the question they should address, not to suggest to the Court that we've known for some time. It is as my learned friend Mr. Thayer said, a tactical decision that they've made, and they should learn to live with it. If they decided to file the motion as each person who was known to be deceased and we've had one that's been deceased (redacted), they should have filed a motion immediately. Instead they've waited and they've waited until the eve of their case in chief for only one reason and that is to cause prejudice to the accused. We strongly object to their motion. We'll write it. We will appreciate the Court's guidance on accepting our briefs at the time indicated to the Rules. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think you need to respond to this latter part of Mr. Ostojic's intervention or submission. I think that forms part of whatever they wish -- they may wish to include in their responses. If there is anything else you wish to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was just hoping that when I stood up he would take a breath for a moment and I was going to object and say that given your Court's ruling you've just handed down, this could all be in writing at the proper time. Could we go into private session for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back into open session. Butler. Now, there are other matters that we would like to raise, but I think we can leave them till Monday. And particular, there is one motion that goes -- Tuesday, sorry. There is one motion, Mr. McCloskey, which goes back to some time that relates to the witness that you have now withdrawn, Vasic, and that again was a motion to amend the 65 ter list of documents which you can safely withdraw from the registry. It's still there. Rather than giving us the trouble of having to declare it moot, you can withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey -- I'm sorry, Mr. Bourgon. My apologies to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, just quickly. I'd just like to confirm which line was requested to be redacted? I missed the line and it's not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I can -- I can tell you. It's -- in my transcript it's page 84, line 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't necessarily mean that it corresponds with yours, but that's what I have. Now, the understanding is we'll sit till a quarter to 2.00. We go straight now to quarter to 3.00. Okay, so we will be sitting till quarter to 3.00 now and hopefully -- will you make an effort, Mr. McCloskey, to finish Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, I am just authorising the filing of an order that will extend the end of the Prosecution case from the 1st of February, that's today, till the 7th of February, and that's when you need to conclude your -- your case, Mr. McCloskey. Up to the 7th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. President, I know Mr. Josse and I have spoken about an issue that he wanted to clarify with Mr. Butler. Perhaps if he just does it right now that would be easier and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think if Mr. Josse is in agreement, we can do that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am. Thank you. Further cross-examination by Mr. Josse:

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, there were two issues. Both can be dealt with very, very briefly. The first relates to my client General Gvero's record and in particular operational duties that he'd undertaken. I think it's right you confused him with another accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct. I was looking at his record and Colonel Pandurevic or General Pandurevic's side by side and I had inadvertently attributed one of Pandurevic's commands to Gvero. So I do concur with Defence that General Gvero appears to, at this juncture from the documents we have, commanded nothing larger than a platoon at this thing. So I think we're accurate on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the second issue relates to Colonel Djordjic and I expect the problem might be my pronunciation. You were getting him confused with a Djordjevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And going back over this Main Staff document that I have, once we got the right translation of the name I clearly see where he does sit and he is not an individual who by position is subordinate to either General Miletic [Realtime transcript read in error "Milosevic"] or General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't think I need to spend any more time on the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I correct the transcript. Line 21, page 87. I think it was the General Miletic and not Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much for that Madam Fauveau. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I express the Trial Chamber's gratitude to Prosecution and Defence teams. We have all agreed to try and bring your testimony to an end today and thus enable you to return home after such a long period here which must have been very strenuous for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, just to be able to advise you that, you know, being prudent I did in fact check with my home agency and if necessary I can be available for the early part of next week. So I mean there are no external drivers to my leaving. I am here at the disposal of the Court as long as I need to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I hope that doesn't send out the message that you have got masochistic tendencies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been working for this organisation for a long time. I think that's long out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey will re-examine you go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler while we're on the topic of correcting some of your remembrances which I know was difficult, I want to take you back to the -- just briefly to the intercept between Jokic and Viletic and I think you had said that you had thought that Mr. Jokic had identified that person as Miletic and we reviewed his transcripts and he said he didn't remember. So --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I stand corrected on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you must be thinking of someone else on that point. If you remember who it was, maybe we'll find out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly I attribute it to him so I guess don't remember at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well. All right. Now, I want to first take you to, as you know, you on cross were talk -- were questioned about the security branch and the October 1994 document. I just want to ask you. Would a brigade chief of security, if he was informed of an operation to -- to detain, transfer, and kill prisoners, would he have a duty under the rules as you knew them to report that fact to his commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on a number of levels I would say yes. I mean, certainly with respect to killing the prisoners it goes back to the obligations of not following law -- orders that are unlawful at face value. So I mean, that's at the first level. I mean, other issues with respect to the detention and transfer, those are not functions that a security officer in and of himself can accomplish with the resources at his disposal. He is going to have to, as a matter of practicality, coordinate these issues with his appropriate commander in order -- if for no other reason than to get access to the materials that he needs or the resources that he needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And taking you briefly to that October 1994 Mladic document, was there anything in that document that would undercut this chief of security's duty or obligation to inform his commander of such information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean I -- again, it goes back to the definition of what a counter-intelligence job or counter-intelligence mission is or is not, and certainly I think that my reading of the JNA materials reflects the fact that dealing -- you know, issues dealing with prisoners of war are not a counter-intelligence function. They are a command function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. In a similar question, does anything about that -- that 94 document provide the chief of security for the corps any authority to prevent the chief of security for the brigade to report that up the chain to his commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand the -- the chain of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try to slow down. Does the -- does that document provide the chief of security of the corps any authority to prevent the duty of the brigade security officer that we have just talked about to report those --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't believe it does. Again in this juncture because those functions are not counter-intelligence functions. They are functions of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you've also -- you've already talked about the -- the duty of a brigade commander to take disciplinary measures again the chief of security. Does -- do you see anything in Mladic's instructions that would interfere with that and what you've already talked about? I don't want to go over the ability of the corps commander or the brigade commander to initiate actions against a chief of security that was committing some sort of crime or infraction.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, it lays out the process to be followed. It doesn't say that it can't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd like to go to 65 ter 426. You talked about the military lexicon, the JNA, this big red book, I think you've referred to where you got the definition of asanacija. You spoke about that with Mr. Haynes. I just want to get that up on the screen and make sure that you've been -- we know what you're talking about. Page 4 in the B/C/S and page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. That's the -- that's the Krstic exhibit that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That defined what you were talking about. Okay. Thank you. All right. Now, Mr. Haynes also mentioned -- had you confirm that you had not talked to Vinko Pandurevic. Were you aware that Vinko Pandurevic had made any -- any comments to Eileen Gilleece about your report, especially the -- your comments about the 15 July interim combat report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And would the killing of 20 or 30 pigs in -- amount -- and cleaning -- cleaning them up from a battlefield area, would that amount to asanacija to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
