utterances.text: A technical sense it would be. In the practical sense of reporting it up to the corps commander, I don't see it as reasonable under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Particularly those circumstances that existed on 15 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Haynes also talked to you about your -- your issue where you basically said Vinko Pandurevic still retained command of the Zvornik Brigade even though he was -- was out of the zone, and you had mentioned that -- I won't go through all your answer, you'd mentioned hearing information of Colonel Trivic from the 2nd Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I've got a statement, Colonel Trivic made in an interview on 24 January 2002, that I don't think you were part of but I want to -- want to run this by you to see if you agree or disagree with what he's saying and how it may incorporate into your answers to Mr. Haynes. And it's -- I'll just -- I'll just read this out. We're talking about Mirko Trivic's chief of staff who is Vidovic Radovan, a lieutenant colonel, and I ask: "And when he was in command of the unit when you were in Srebrenica, what were his responsibilities? I mean, did he have the same responsibilities as the commander?" Mirko Trivic says: "You're entering a topic that someone can write a Ph.D. on. He had the right to make decisions. He had the right to make decisions that would not interrupt the status in the zone without consulting me, and anything that would disrupt the system that was established or was threatening to disrupt the system he had to report to me. He had to report to me and then eventually make some suggestions that is this or that should be done and based on my answer, approval or disapproval, he was supposed to act." Now, apart from that statement about the Ph.D., how does this comment --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, how can you take out the comment of the Ph.D.? It's an intrinsic part of what Colonel Trivic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can agree that it's a good document for Ph.D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think technically he's -- Mr. Haynes is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you want Mr. Butler to comment on the Ph.D.? I'm just asking him not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not necessarily, but the objection is that you are extracting that part and asking Mr. Butler or leaving him no choice to comment on that if he wishes to. So I would suggest that you proceed with referring him to the entire, and if he wants to comment on that he comments. If he doesn't, he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can you comment on -- on this at all as it fits into your analysis, especially going back to your discussion on this point with Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, it is a -- it dovetails with my understanding about the rules of command, you know, as they were applied in the JNA -- or as they were written in the JNA regulations and applied by the VRS at the time. I place much weight on that particularly given the fact that at the time Colonel Trivic was a contemporary of Colonel Pandurevic. And with respect to where he was and what he was doing, he was in the identical command situation of Colonel Pandurevic down at Srebrenica with the operations of his brigade in his brigade zone being controlled by his chief of staff. So I give that great weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on. You were asked about the presence of General Mladic on the 14th, and you talked about him being in Belgrade. And can we go to 65 ter 532. And as that's coming up, do you recall a General Elliot?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you take a brief look at this statement of General Elliot. Does that have anything to do with your conclusion about the whereabouts of General Mladic on the 14th and 15th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does. It is in large part what I base my knowledge on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. You also spoke -- you were asked about the relationship between the VRS and the Presidency, and I think you spoke briefly of the -- President Karadzic trying to fire General Mladic. Can we go to document 65 ter 3160. And as that's coming up, Mr. Butler, you will see that it's a 5 August 1995 from the Main Staff under the name of General Mladic. And I don't want to go into this in detail, but we can see that its entitled "Renaming of the Main Staff of the VRS as the General Staff" and more importantly for my purposes "and the appointment of General Mladic as special advisor to the Supreme Commander." Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just briefly as you can, what does it, if anything does it have to do with your testimony about Karadzic firing -- trying to fire Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at this point in time as a way of trying to fire Mladic essentially what they're doing is kicking him upstairs. They're taking him out of the command of the VRS or attempting to and making him a special advisor which essentially strips him of all command authority over the army. As part of this, the Main Staff and a number of the general officers as well as a number of the corps commanders refused to follow this order and in fact published a letter, an open letter, back to the president reaffirming their support of General Mladic. In effect, you know, I guess the phrase is mutiny, where they took them -- you know, they essentially collectively disavowed that they were going to follow an order from their commander-in-chief or in this case the Supreme Commander. It was about a month and a half crisis before it was finally resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 1026. And this is from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, 5-6 August 1995 to the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, to the President of Republika Srpska. Again we don't need to get into this in detail, but is this what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is from the generals?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If we look at -- let's go to page 2 of the English. Basically the first page is a statement in support of General Mladic. And we see the people that are on it, Mladic, Milovanovic, Gvero, Djukic, Tolimir, Skrbic. I won't read all of them. I don't see General Miletic on this. Do you have any information, any clear information about -- about why General Miletic isn't on this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's not the only the general that's not on it but I don't know why he's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And on the same subject, did President Karadzic ever initiate any kind of investigation involving the events of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm aware of two, one of them which was initiated by President Karadzic which I believe was either late 1995 or early 1996, and there was also an investigation initiated by the military prosecutor's office at approximately March or April of 1996. So they may have been under the umbrella of the one investigation but those are two I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 22. It talks about a -- starting an investigation to investigate the discovery of two bodies at Pilica. Is this one of the things you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 21. Well, which one? It's obvious, but let's go to 65 ter 21 now.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which -- I mean, this is the order by the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And now at 65 ter 21, this is a 1 April document. Do you know how this document relates to the previous document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's a supplemental part of it, I mean although this one, I believe, is more affiliated with the Main Staff and military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now let's go to 65 ter 23. And that first page that we see in B/C/S is 23 September, and it -- it says: "Enclosed here with is a report of the Ministry of Interior with information concerning the period when Srebrenica was liberated. Minister Dragan Kijac." And then we see the body of it the next -- on the next page. The B/C/S body -- should be page 2 of the B/C/S. There we go. What is this, Mr. Butler, briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is the two components that were investigating. One was the military prosecutor's office. The other one was the MUP, the civilian -- the Ministry of the Interior, I should say. And this is the report from the Ministry of Interior on the results of their investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what's the gist of their results?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I recall correctly, the gist of their results was something along the lines of "We found no evidence that the army did anything and it is our conclusion that the Muslims probably killed themselves."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, there's a bit more in there about that but I won't get into it. All right. You'd also talked about Hotel Fontana receipts that you had thought Mr. Beara might have been on one of them and then you said that you didn't think he was on one of them, so I've got the Hotel Fontana receipts for you to go through briefly so we can clarify that. 65 ter 457. And if we could -- yeah. Let's just give you the whole -- we've got a folder of some of these, Mr. Butler. This is on tab 10. And just to clarify it, I think your second recollection was better, that he was -- that he is not -- having reviewed this, Beara is not on these documents. But a few people are, so just to clarify what this is, can you go to page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you make of this? It says 31 July on it and we see some people's names on it, especially Colonel Popovic. Do you recall what your analysis of this resulted in or ...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It corresponds to how many days these individuals had a room at the Hotel Fontana. And of course the practice was the military would stay there and that at the end of each particular month the Hotel Fontana would send a bill to the Bratunac Brigade to be paid. This was a common practice not only for the month of July but many of the other officers of the Bratunac Brigade who didn't have houses there also stayed at the Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I think we can state for the record there is no mention of Mr. Beara on this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right I'm not going to ask you any more about it. Let's go to the area where I think it was Ms. Fauveau was asking but the -- I think it was a May document from Milovanovic talking about taking UN hostages and she was asking you about potential Drina Corps involvement in that and you had said you had inferred Drina Corps involvement in some of it. Let's go to 65 ter 3161 to try to clear up that issue a bit. Sorry, that's -- yes, 3161. This is a 27 May document from the Drina Corps in the name of General Zivanovic, and it does -- I'm sorry, I guess we need a little help with Mr. ELMO. We can see it does make reference to the Main Staff order of 27 May, 03-4/1037. And I want to take you to the next page, page 2 in the English, and it lists the number of -- number of Drina Corps brigades to get involved in this. And if we can go down. Have you had a chance to see this document before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I may have during proofing, but I just don't recall at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then let me just call your attention to the -- it says: "The 1st Zvornik Brigade have two members at the command post and the BRAG firing positions." What does this -- how does this fit into your conclusions to Ms. Fauveau about the Drina Corps involvement in this UN hostage business?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I mean, again, it is all the issue of the fact that it was clear a little bit earlier in this where they were talking about, you know, When you take UN people into custody, here's how your going to deploy them out. So obviously they were a part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to avoid to have -- this order of General Zivanovic has to do with something with something very specific, so I would like to see paragraph 1 of the order of Mr. Zivanovic in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we see it in English, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have it in English first of all? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise for going through this quickly. I would normally have spent more time on it. But there it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Fauveau needs to see page 1 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But when she says page 1, I assume it's from the very beginning. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I need indeed to see paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you scroll -- yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could the witness tell us in which region or area is the place where the prisoners were to be taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau, thank you. Mr. McCloskey -- Mr. Butler, first of all, are you in a position to answer or give us information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe if you scroll down or scroll to page 2 it lays that out, talking about -- it's the 5th Podrinje shall capture and disarm UN members blocked in that particular area. They will in sequence notify the command, the 5th BVP is, of course, the 5th military police battalion who will take them over and then the Drina Corps distributes them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed with your next question, Mr. McCloskey, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 3162 to see if there was any action taken on this Drina Corps order. This is a Zvornik Brigade daily combat report to the command of the Drina Corps, and -- I hope it's in e-court. Okay. And it's what we've become used to seeing and as it's coming up I'll just start looking at a bullet point under bullet point 3, and it says: "In the brigade ZO," zone of operations, I believe, "there are two UNPROFOR members who were captured in the area of Gorazde. They are being treated pursuant to instructions from the command of the Drina Corps." What does this indicate to you, Mr. Butler, relating to these orders that we've been looking at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I ask you to go to page 2 of the English document, please. I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. So everyone can see that. That is on page 2. Up at the top.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I guess because of the time sequence, I mean, I -- it's related to that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another area. Mr. Lazarevic was asking you questions about the locations of various PJP units and other MUP units on the important days of the 12th and 13th of July and you did make some reference to reviewing certain documents. What I want to ask you is did you -- did you review 65 ter number 92, which as it comes up is a -- is a report that has no front page and a scrawled -- the scrawled name of Borovcanin on the back? Is this a report that you've had a chance to review?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall where this report came from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vaguely. I wouldn't want to speculate on -- on the origins of it. I mean I think I remember, but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. This is the subject matter of a stipulation between myself and Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. President, that we would stipulate that this -- this report was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by Mr. Vasic during the investigation and that it is not complete because there's pages -- there are clearly pages that are not there that you will be able to see when you examine it. And the name on the bottom of it, Ljubisa Borovcanin, is not the signature of -- of the accused in this case but that it is a report -- Mr. Lazarevic from him. Mr. Lazarevic if he has anything to add or clarify or object to, I would invite him to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I can very briefly explain. I had a conversation with Mr. McCloskey earlier this morning regarding this document because I noticed that he intends to use this document in re-examination of Mr. Butler, and indeed we did stipulate that this document is not complete, that there are pages missing, that it is signed -- it bears the signature Ljubisa Borovcanin, but that actually that this is not the hand signature of Mr. Borovcanin. But there are a couple of other things that I wanted to ask Mr. Butler since I didn't have the opportunity to ask Mr. Vasic, who was supposed to testify on this document since he was withdrawn from Prosecution list. So the only point that I wanted to make at this time is to just to ask the Trial Chamber to allow me three, literally three questions to Mr. Butler regarding this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you will need to allow five minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps we can do it right now as we're on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If there is no objection. Yes, go ahead, Mr. Lazarevic. Further cross-examination by Mr. Lazarevic:

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Butler, do you see this document before you, P0092? And of course you can look at the English version, page 1 of the document.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Registrar scrolled me to page 1 on the -- yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you see who the document was sent to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may have to scroll up a little bit further. It's not evident from -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course you can look at the entire document, but I'm telling you that there is not a single trace that would indicate who the document is addressed to or sent to.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it doesn't appear in -- I don't know that I can infer that from where it would be going from the actual body, you know, but somebody's making a report. I don't know who they're reporting to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm also putting to you that neither this document nor any other piece of evidence points to the period of time when the document -- this document was made. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, well, it -- it contextually discusses the time period. I don't think that there is anything in the document which tells us when it was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There is one other thing I want to put to you. Nowhere in this document is the title thereof contained. In other words, regular combat report or interim combat report, any title of that sort; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment before you answer that question. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was just stretching my legs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's an innovation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean -- again, I guess because of whomever provided it - I guess it would be Vasic - there appears to be some of the normal report header data excised out. So it is, I agree, it's impossible to tell. It's not consistent with, for example, the Vasic documents that we have where he's reporting back up his chain on events where you have the normal MUP corresponding numbers and everything else. So it is definitely in this sense, you know, a block of context with nothing surrounding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. Thank you, Mr. Butler. I have no other questions on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Further re-examination by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 3163 and this is an area where Ms. Fauveau was talking to you about the whereabouts of General Miletic. She said specifically from the 2nd to the 12th of July. And are you familiar with some of the statements of General Milanovic talking about where he was, where Milanovic was, and -- and where Miletic was in the period of -- in July generally?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if General Milovanovic had been interviewed while I was still here. I think I know a general thrust of his story but I don't think I'm really familiar with the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If you could just take a look, let's go to page 2 of this document. It's a short information report from General Milovanovic and where he has been provided the -- from 1995 all the daily combat reports from the Main Staff to the Presidency in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor and has checked the -- as you can see from the document, checked to see whose name they went out under and has noted that down there. And if we could -- let's -- let's go to our period of time. I think it's on the second -- or third page of the English. 31 May through September 4. All those ERNs were type signed by Radivoje Miletic. Does this correspond with information you have about where Milovanovic was at this time period, May through September --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before you answer, Mr. Butler. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at this stage of the procedure the Defence of General Miletic does not contest the fact that this document, it's a report, it's a regular report of the situation on the front, on the lines, and this would have been written with the type written name of General Miletic, but because of the testimony of this expert witness who says when there isn't the letters SR to mean read personally, he cannot affirm that he was there. We do not contest the fact that the report for that period was in the name of General Miletic. Perhaps this could expedite a bit the questioning by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it may. If she doesn't object to this document going into evidence and I can clarify a couple of issues on what she has just said and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I saw her nodding. She wouldn't object.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you may perhaps take her advice and act on her suggestion and move forward. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, given what you have testified to about these type signed things and what she just said, nevertheless would identifying when a document goes out under General Miletic's name, especially a study of all these documents, would that assist an investigator or an analyst like yourself in -- in determining where a person was working or whether in fact they were working on the issues in the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, sir. I mean, you know, granted in many cases we've heard, you know, the names go out but maybe it is a subordinate who is authorised to sign for them. But the fact this those documents are going out under is that particular individual's name again is a reflection that that person is performing his function, and that's why I mean from the VRS perspective they -- they -- for whatever the reason, they differentiated the responsibilities so that when General Milovanovic wasn't performing his functions at the headquarters in -- at the Main Staff headquarters that these documents were going out under General Miletic. So it meant something to them and as a result they differentiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Ms. Fauveau did specifically mention on her cross documents from 2 to 12 July and we have spoken and she has agreed that we can offer those into evidence, those, and I will have a list of those and not take Mr. Butler through all of them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Butler, another -- try to get through this quickly. When you're testifying about Potocari a bit, you -- you made a statement that you -- I'll try to paraphrase it. You didn't see in the reporting chains what you knew to be going on or what we knew to be going on in Potocari. You didn't see that through the reporting chain of the military. That was pretty vague. What do you mean by that, I mean, given that you and I went through each of those documents.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I -- to be clear you didn't see, for example, in great detail the situations as being described -- I mean, the Bratunac daily combat reports or the Zvornik, you know -- well, particularly with Potocari with the Bratunac. You got a glimpse perhaps. But information was going up and certainly I think perhaps the clearest view of what you get is the 13 July report by Colonel Jankovic going up to his higher headquarters, or in this case it would be the Main Staff, reporting on the large nuggets of data with respect to the completion of moving people out and what the situation is on the ground at Potocari. You also had to some degree with respect to the convoys you had telephonic which is the intercepts information going up the chain of command, but what you didn't see going up the chain of command is issues related to separations or things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's -- there was also discussion with Ms. Fauveau about 155 and whose extension that might have been or what number that was and -- and let's -- if we could go to 65 ter 3175, I'll try to get through this. I'm not sure it's a document you've seen, but it's dated 17 May 1995. It's -- you can see it's from the Bosnian army. And to briefly summarise it, it appears the Bosnian army laid in ambush and killed two Serb soldiers and received some paper on them with General Mladic's and others' names on them with extensions next to their -- or numbers next to their name. Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would this be something that would be of any value to you in determining this issue of phone numbers and who was at what extension?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would in the sense that it confirmed information and as I'm trying to scroll through it real fast, given the place where it appears that the information was -- was captured or the information was taken from the soldiers who were ambushed, I think the location, it actually corresponds with an area that the members of the communications regiment would have been doing guard duty around the headquarters. So as a member of a communication regiment, he may very well had more detailed information on these phone numbers than your average soldier might have expected. So there is a sense of credibility to this, and certainly when we would dovetail this against the phone numbers that we would have in various Republika Srpska or VRS documents that list that, I mean, it would tend to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you another Exhibit 3176 that we found recently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to object because I think we're losing time. The documents 155 are talking about the documents on which General Milovanovic gave testimony for some time, document 30/5, and this was shown to General Milovanovic and was not. So I don't really see why now this should be examined by this witness, the witness we have now. This does not sustain the arguments during the direct examination, so I really don't see what we're doing now. This being said, I do not oppose to the exhibit we now have here, the one which has just been commented upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey do you wish to comment on that on the basis that it's not unusual that the same document is shown to different witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The exhibit I'm about to show which I think drew the objection is this Main Staff phone book and I do not have it as something that's in evidence and if she has no objection to it going into evidence we can get through it rather quickly, but it does specifically respond to the issue of who was at 155 which was a big issue on cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This would not be a problem, but for -- about 155, but this number, has this number been used, and in this conversation is it -- this is just a phone number of the -- I think it's perfectly clear. It's the phone number of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can argue about what it means but she's opened this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, the witness has already testified on that number, saying that it's an extension, according to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I've got the Main Staff phone book which I think will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, precisely. There have been so many witnesses here who were members of the Main Staff, and the Prosecutor had these exhibits. So why were they not given to those people who were in a better position to appraise this, the question of the telephone book. Perhaps it was never seen by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It can become an argument later on, Ms. Fauveau. Let's proceed. Let's proceed. Go ahead, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, B/C/S page 16, English page 2. Again, Mr. Butler, I don't know if you've had chance to see this document before. I just became aware of it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I don't recall having that document available to me during my tenure here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we need to go down to near the bottom of the page where it's entitled "Chief of staff." And this thing was dated, I think I saw August of 1995, and we see, again, is this just -- and I know this is a quick review, but does this assist your analysis on the 155 issue?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It certainly -- it confirms the earlier views that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. All right. Let me continue. There was also questions from Ms. Fauveau about directive 7 to you and especially the part about the Drina Corps, the last part, and she asked you something related to whether that last part was part of the old JNA All People's Defence or something -- something like that, but let me read this out to you: "By planned and well-thought out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Aside from this reference in directive 7 which of course comes from the level it came from, are you aware of a brigade or a lower echelon document that makes a very similar statement to this in regard to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If I recall there's a Bratunac Brigade document that reads if not the same language somewhere along the same lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 3177. It is a 4 July 1994, Bratunac Brigade report for the brigade members and it is in the name of the then commander Slavko Ognjenovic. And I just want to refer you to -- it should be page 3 in the English, and it's under paragraph 2 in the B/C/S, but it's at the end of -- the very end of paragraph 2 in the B/C/S, and it says: "There will be no retreat when it comes to Srebrenica enclave. We must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible realising that they cannot survive there." Is that the thing you remembered?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's the terminology I remember from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Getting to the area of General Gvero. Mr. Josse went through with you in some detail your views and his questions related to the morale part of the job and the -- your view of the propaganda part of the job, and we've been able to find some documents outside of the July '95 time frame in the name of General Gvero, and if we could go -- I want to ask you about them. 3179 would be the first one, and if you could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think I'll make the objection now if I may. I mean, Mr. McCloskey was good enough to alert us to this yesterday. Your Honour, briefly, when I cross-examined on this issue on the 30th of January at page 20677, I conceded in the course of the cross-examination that propaganda may have been part of the issue transcript and the transcript says import of morale, but what you should have said is that they dealt with morale, not propaganda. In other words, at no point was I suggesting that propaganda was not part of the job nor did I ever suggest that it wasn't an important part of the job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, you had dealt with that area as well in the course of your cross-examination of a previous witness. I am not mentioning his name. It starts with a T, precisely because I can't remember whether he was a protected witness or not. But in any case, let's hear the question because we haven't heard the question as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have basically two documents that were in Mr. Gvero's name. The first is dated 8 February 1993. It's entitled report of the state of morale in the army of Republika Srpska. Mr. Butler, if you could look at the entire document. It should be in your tab 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President -- my intention would be to ask Mr. Butler to review this as briefly as he can and ask him to -- if it clarifies or responds to the questions and the insinuations that were brought up by my colleague. He questioned him at length about the morale job and the propaganda job, and he attacked him very hard on his -- Mr. Butler's emphasis on propaganda. So I think this is an area that I absolutely have the right to get into. I'm not going to spend long on it, I don't want him to evaluate the whole document, but they spent a lot of time on this issue and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In two sentences, my cross-examination went to the emphasis of the report on propaganda rather than morale. The witness conceded that morale as opposed to propaganda was as important perhaps more important than propaganda and he explained why he'd emphasised propaganda over morale. That's something the Trial Chamber will need to decide in due course. This doesn't take the matter any further in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me take you right back to the question so that you have the full -- it goes -- you may recall this. He said: "First and foremost this staff element was responsible for managing the information/propaganda campaign and the support of the war aims." And that's a quote from Mr. Butler's report. And then Mr. Josse says: "That's not true, is it?" Mr. Butler says: "I believe it is." He says: "You are saying that the main role of the sector was propaganda rather than morale, are you?" "Propaganda is a tool by which people use, you know, information in order to impact morale. It's -- it's a component part of how it's done. It's not a separate issue." "Question: That may be right, but first and foremost that sector dealt with morale. Propaganda may have been part of the issue and an import of morale but what you should have said there is that they dealt with morale, not propaganda. You said propaganda because it sounds worse. That's the truth, Mr. Butler, isn't it?" I mean, that kind of attack clearly opens the door to his client's documents on morale and propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Have you finished your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, I'd like him to take a look at this document because what I've done is I've tried to find a -- what appears to be a morale document and ask him about that to see if -- what he says about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I know it's a quick read, Mr. Butler, but as we see this it's a report on the state of morale in the army of Republika Srpska, dated 8 February 1993, is -- in your brief review of this report, does it fit with your testimony and your report on -- on what you believe this branch to be all about or partly about, I should say.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean yes, sir. I guess maybe the easiest way to get my point across is if you go to page 11 of the English language version of this. I mean, it -- it talks about the point that I tried to make. I mean, that -- that propaganda is a means, is a tool by which morale is influenced, and in fact that particular paragraph notes that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. It also mentioned some three quality papers, Srpska Vojska. What's that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- Srpska Vojska is the military magazine of the army of the Republika Srpska. It was published monthly, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was did -- who was it supposed to go to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The target audience was the soldiers of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can we go to page 8 of the English. And I'm sorry, I don't -- but I don't think -- we may not -- basically, this document goes through factual situations in each of the corps and here we see something about the Drina Corps, and it talks about specific territory, towns, information. How is it that the morale officer would be aware of this kind of information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the morale -- or I don't want to say the morale officer because it's more than that, but the assistant commander for morale at the various levels has to have a clear understanding of what's been happening and why because he's required to integrate his work into that in order to support these specific issues, to be able to look at what has happened on the ground and be able to highlight the positive things they want to be able to emphasise for their soldiers. I mean, he's got to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 3180 and this is an article dated 15 July 1993. It says author Major General Milan Gvero. This is from the publication of Srpska Vojska and the subject is: Gvero describes the just struggle waged by Serbs in Bosnia. It's entitled, Silk Cord for Alija. I'm not going to read all of it but if we could all take a look at this. It starts out: "The defensive and national liberation war waged by the Serbs in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina has been underway for 16 months. Everyone knows that the Serbs did not want this war and that they did everything possible to prevent it. The Serbs are well acquainted with the horrors and hells of war. In the past they took part in all wars in these parts and always suffered the greatest losses. They were victors and they were on the side of the victors. In peacetime, their fate was that of the defeated. They could not express themselves as Serbs so as not to violate the pride of the few around them. But in this war which they did not want and which was imposed on them, the Serbs had no choice. They had to fight or disappear. They had to fight or face the suffering and humility and death in large numbers. It was a question of fighting or assent by the survivors of the now vengeful sinister Asiatic Turkish oppression and constant threats by Ustasha knives and in Ustasha pits. Exceptionally peace loving, tolerant and dignified the noble and honourable Serbian people chose the path of self-preservation to defend themselves and everything that makes a nation worthy of respect. A nation of peace and tolerance --" I won't go on. There's more similar and in the end it describes how a silk cord would be used by the -- Alija Izetbegovic's own people to pull around his neck and tighten it. What is this? Does this have any function or object and, if so, what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean setting aside the actual language component, it -- it addresses what I had discussed earlier was the fact that, you know, part of the object of the maintenance and upkeep of morale that -- that all modern militaries want to be able to do is to be able to have the soldiers share the values and the goals of the institution that they're fighting for. One of the re-occurring themes that goes through the Serb propaganda and the military propaganda has always been the theme that we are fighting a defensive war because if we don't fight this war, you know, the spectre of genocide will be on us. And clearly given the historical context of what happened there, it is going to be a powerful metaphor, and that's going to evoke a reaction. This was one of the many themes that was placed out there by the army as an attempt to get the soldiers, who weren't necessarily buying into the political cause, to buy into at least the necessity of having to fight to defend values that they were more in tune with, their families and their houses and their very existence. So this is -- this is propaganda 101 for lack of a better phrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, just to make sure you are aware of this, you have only got 10 minutes left or, rather, we have only got 10 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Understood, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, let's go to 65 ter 3184. This is a 21 September 1995 document from the sector on morale, religious and legal affairs and this I'm asking you about because Mr. Josse was at some point was questioning you about when you mentioned military courts and Mr. Gvero's responsibility there he asked -- he was questioning why -- why you would bring that up, because that had been moved over to the Ministry of Defence, and you had an answer on that point. And I would like you to just take a look at this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. May I consult my client just for a minute? I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in the meantime, but let's proceed. In the meantime, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Butler, if you could take a look at that and I especially would call your attention to page 6 --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me what tab it is in mine?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, it should be tab 4. The very last one. Sorry, the very last one in your book.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If you could take a look at that and it's again full of lots of information about the ongoing situation. So try to catch up as best you can. I only have one more document after this, but if we go to what is 3 -- 3 (c) in the B/C/S, and it's page 6, paragraph (c). This section began on page 5 by saying: "In view of the requirements of the current combat situation and the objectives of the struggle of the Serbian people, the following measures must immediately be taken in commands and units at all levels." And it says various things. We get to (c) it says: "Raise the level of responsibilities of the officers for building discipline in units, raising the level of discipline particularly in commands of all levels. Immediately take appropriate measures for all cases of indiscipline that might have negative consequences for the execution of combat assignments and the lives of personnel." And this is what I wanted to ask you about "immediately activate special military courts at brigade level in order to protect the authority of the command system and discipline, and to prevent personnel from leaving the units and other negative occurrences." How does that fit into your answers to his previous questions on this point when you were challenged?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this particular context, and it's provided for under law wherein a declaration of the state of war is made, there is a provision under law at the brigade level, literally that low, can essentially put together its own military court and it's for summary judgement. It is a negative motivational tool to be used to try soldiers accused of deserting under fire, cowardice, things of that nature. I mean, there's positive motivating of the soldiers and negative motivational factors. When we talk about the military justice system in most countries, we can't lose sight of the fact that justice is one goal of it and the maintenance of good order and discipline is another goal of it. And these special military courts are part of the tools that a commander had at these times in his arsenal to ensure that the soldiers, you know, would not shirk from their duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the last document. Going -- 4 August 1995, 65 ter 3182, your tab -- third from the last, I believe. 4 August 1995 document.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Got it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again it's -- it's from General Gvero under his name to various corps and other units describing the situation, and what I wanted to ask you about in particular is -- starts on the bottom of page 3 and is related to the topic you just mentioned. It says: "Unfortunately, even some members of the army sometimes do not know what to do in a situation where the population temporarily leaves the territory or in a more fierce enemy attack and they too pass on and spread certain rumours that have the effect of unsettling the population and units. All such members of the army and civilians who play a part in passing on and spreading rumours shall be identified and prosecuted, and a special unit will be made up of these people to be used in the most complex combat situations." All right. Well, we see prosecution. You've referred to that as one negative inspiration. What do you make of this putting people in complex -- the assistant commander for morale, legal and religious sending this out? What is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all part of the -- I mean, it's all part of the message that's going down to the soldiers and -- and their officers reminding them that, you know, they have to use all of the tools at their disposal. I mean, particularly in the context of the crisis that's now occurring, you know, letting them now use all the tools at your disposal in order to maintain good order and discipline among the troops. And in my narratives -- not my narratives but in my brigade and corps combat reports I believe I discuss the actual mechanics of these summary military courts in detail so I won't get into them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Butler, thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours and everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, all long journeys finally come to an end and yours is one of them. I can't thank you enough for having been so patient with all of us. You've been here for almost a month. I don't know if you have established a record, I'm not quite sure, but in any case, we are very thankful and grateful for your availability and for your testimony. I'm sure everyone will join me in wishing you a very safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll deal with the documents on Tuesday, not now, because I don't know what to expect so I would rather -- yes, Mr. Bourgon. Thank you, Mr. Butler you will now be escorted and given the assistance you require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, very quickly. [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Regarding the admissibility of documents, Mr. President, we would like to proceed at least on behalf of the accused Drago Nikolic in two different segments and to submit our arguments in writing concerning the admissibility of the reports of Mr. Butler. So I'll just say that as an advance issue that we'd like to discuss on Monday. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not on Monday, on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On Tuesday, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we stand adjourned until Tuesday afternoon. It's Tuesday afternoon. In the meantime, please be informed that we have extended, officially extended the end of the Prosecution case till the 7th. Thank you. One moment. I also wish to thank all the staff, the technicians, the recorders, the interpreters. I know what all this means to you to sit here for an extra -- to stay here for an extra hour and a half on a Friday, and of course to everyone else thank you so much, and I want to make sure that this is also conveyed to the superiors in each category to so that they are aware of our appreciation. Thank you. Have a nice weekend all of you.
